Malaria remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in sub-Saharan Africa, and the emergence of partial artemisinin resistance in Plasmodium falciparum, now documented in Rwanda, Uganda and Eritrea, underscores the urgent need for new chemotypes with novel mechanisms of action. In this study, we report the discovery and optimization of a series of 2-aminopyrazolo[1,5-a]pyrimidines identified through a phenotypic screen of 48,000 compounds against the asexual blood stage of P. falciparum 3D7.

The initial hit, compound 1 (EC50 = 410 nM), displayed modest potency and poor metabolic stability in human liver microsomes (intrinsic clearance of 86 µL/min/mg). Through iterative structure-activity relationship studies encompassing 112 analogues, we identified key structural features governing both potency and stability. Replacement of the metabolically labile N-benzyl group with a 4-fluoro-cyclohexylmethyl substituent, together with the introduction of a pyridyl nitrogen at the 6-position, yielded compound 37, which exhibited an EC50 of 12 nM against 3D7 and retained full activity against the multidrug-resistant Dd2 and K1 strains as well as Cam3.II harbouring the Kelch13 R539T mutation. Compound 37 showed favourable selectivity over HepG2 cells (selectivity index greater than 2,000), low clearance in human and mouse microsomes, and an aqueous solubility of 74 µM at pH 7.4.

In the P. berghei mouse model, a single oral dose of 30 mg/kg reduced parasitaemia by 99.2% on day 4 post-infection, and a four-dose regimen at 10 mg/kg resulted in cure in three of five animals. Parasite reduction ratio assays indicated a moderately fast killing profile comparable to chloroquine. In vitro resistance selection and whole-genome sequencing of resistant clones revealed mutations in PfATP4, suggesting that this series shares a target with cipargamin while exhibiting a distinct chemical scaffold and a lower propensity for haemolysis-related liabilities in preliminary assessments.

Taken together, these findings establish the 2-aminopyrazolo[1,5-a]pyrimidine series as a promising starting point for the development of a next-generation antimalarial. Further optimization will focus on improving the predicted human half-life and evaluating transmission-blocking activity against stage V gametocytes, with the overarching goal of delivering a candidate suitable for single-dose combination therapy.

Routine antimicrobial resistance surveillance in much of West Africa still depends on a handful of reference laboratories, and the data they produce rarely reach the clinicians who prescribe. We asked whether a low-cost, decentralised workflow could close part of that gap. Between March 2023 and August 2025 we placed simplified culture and disc-diffusion capacity in 14 district hospitals across Ghana and Burkina Faso, linked to two regional hubs that confirmed isolates by MALDI-TOF and broth microdilution.

Over the study period the network processed 9,812 clinical specimens, mostly blood and urine, and recovered 2,377 bacterial isolates. Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae made up just over half. Third-generation cephalosporin resistance was common: 61% of E. coli and 74% of K. pneumoniae isolates were non-susceptible to ceftriaxone. Carbapenem non-susceptibility was lower but not negligible, at 6.8% for K. pneumoniae, and it clustered in three hospitals with large neonatal units. Whole-genome sequencing of 212 carbapenem-resistant isolates showed that blaOXA-181 and blaNDM-1 dominated, carried on a small number of plasmid backbones that moved between sites within months.

Agreement between district readings and hub confirmation was 91% overall. It dropped to 78% for Acinetobacter, mostly because of breakpoint misreads, and improved after a second round of on-site training. The median time from specimen collection to a report reaching the ward fell from 11 days under the previous referral system to 4 days.

The network is not cheap to run, and its continuation depends on reagent supply chains that faltered twice during the study. Even so, the data were good enough to change practice: two hospitals revised their empirical sepsis protocols for neonates, replacing ampicillin and gentamicin with regimens informed by local susceptibility. We think the main lesson is that surveillance pays for itself only when results come back fast enough to matter at the bedside. Data and analysis code are openly available, and we describe the minimum staffing and supply requirements for other ministries considering a similar model.

Tuberculosis continues to be the leading cause of death from a single infectious agent worldwide, and the increasing prevalence of multidrug-resistant strains requires a steady supply of new chemical matter with clinical potential. In this work, we describe the hit-to-lead progression of a benzimidazole-carboxamide series that was identified in a whole-cell screen against Mycobacterium tuberculosis H37Rv under aerobic and nutrient-starvation conditions.

The original hit, ERS-0412, inhibited bacterial growth with a minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC90) of 3.1 µM but presented high lipophilicity (cLogP 5.4) and rapid degradation in mouse liver microsomes. We synthesised 86 analogues across three regions of the molecule, guided by matched molecular pair analysis and by a cytochrome P450 site-of-metabolism prediction model. Introduction of a morpholine at the 5-position and replacement of the terminal phenyl ring with a 2-methoxypyridine reduced cLogP by 1.8 units and improved microsomal half-life more than fivefold, while maintaining potency. The resulting lead compound, ERS-0587, displayed an MIC90 of 0.39 µM against H37Rv, retained activity against a panel of 18 clinical isolates including isoniazid- and rifampicin-resistant strains, and was bactericidal in a macrophage infection model, reducing intracellular bacterial load by 1.6 log10 CFU after five days.

Spontaneous resistant mutants were raised at a frequency of approximately 10^-8, and whole-genome sequencing identified mutations in mmpL3, which encodes the essential mycolic acid transporter. This mechanism was further supported by accumulation of trehalose monomycolate in treated cultures. Importantly, ERS-0587 showed no significant inhibition of the hERG channel at 30 µM and low cytotoxicity against Vero and HepG2 cells. Pharmacokinetic evaluation in BALB/c mice after oral administration at 25 mg/kg showed an oral bioavailability of 41% and plasma exposure above the MIC for approximately ten hours.

These results demonstrate that careful control of lipophilicity can overcome one of the main limitations frequently associated with MmpL3 inhibitors. ERS-0587 is now being evaluated in an acute murine efficacy model, and the series represents a valuable addition to the tuberculosis drug discovery pipeline.

Accurate prediction of absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion and toxicity (ADMET) properties is essential for reducing late-stage attrition in drug discovery, yet the performance of machine learning models often deteriorates substantially when applied to chemical space that differs from the training data. In this study, we present a systematic benchmark of 14 molecular representations and 6 learning algorithms across 22 ADMET endpoints, with a particular focus on generalisation to structurally novel compounds.

We compiled a curated dataset of approximately 310,000 measurements from ChEMBL, the Therapeutics Data Commons and three publicly released pharmaceutical datasets, applying rigorous standardisation, deduplication and unit harmonisation procedures. Models were evaluated using random, scaffold-based and time-split partitions, as well as a newly proposed cluster-distance split that explicitly controls the Tanimoto similarity between training and test sets. Representations included extended-connectivity fingerprints, RDKit descriptors, Mordred descriptors, pretrained graph neural network embeddings and transformer-based embeddings derived from large chemical language models.

Our results reveal that the apparent superiority of deep learning approaches under random splits largely disappears under more stringent evaluation. Across endpoints, gradient-boosted trees trained on a combination of fingerprints and physicochemical descriptors performed within 0.03 AUROC of the best deep model on average, while requiring considerably less computational resources. Pretrained embeddings offered meaningful advantages for a subset of tasks with limited data, notably hERG inhibition and human hepatocyte clearance, where they improved Spearman correlation by up to 0.11. Performance declined monotonically with decreasing similarity to the training set for all model classes, and calibrated uncertainty estimates obtained via conformal prediction successfully identified the majority of large errors.

These findings highlight the importance of evaluation protocols that reflect real-world prospective use and suggest that model choice should be guided by data availability and the intended applicability domain rather than architectural novelty alone. To facilitate reproducibility and further research, all datasets, splits and trained models have been made publicly available through an open-source repository and can be accessed via a unified command-line interface.

Benznidazole and nifurtimox have been the only drugs for Chagas disease for roughly half a century. Both are poorly tolerated, and neither reliably clears the chronic infection that most patients actually have by the time they are diagnosed. One reason the pipeline has stayed so thin is that Trypanosoma cruzi amastigotes can enter a slow-growing, drug-tolerant state that standard intracellular assays do not capture well.

We built a washout assay to look for compounds that kill these persisters rather than merely suppressing replication. Infected U2OS cells were exposed to compound for 96 hours, washed, and then monitored for parasite regrowth over 14 days by high-content imaging of a fluorescent reporter strain. We screened 2,600 compounds from an annotated kinase-focused library and a set of 400 clinical candidates from other indications.

Most actives in the conventional endpoint did not survive the washout. Of 118 compounds with an IC50 below 1 µM at 96 hours, only 9 prevented regrowth at concentrations under ten times their IC50. Benznidazole itself allowed recrudescence in about a third of wells at 20 µM, which is consistent with what is seen clinically. Two chemotypes stood out. The first, a set of oxaborole analogues, was rapidly cidal in the assay. The second, a series of aminothiazole inhibitors originally developed against human CLK kinases, was slower but produced complete clearance at 2.5 µM, and its activity tracked with inhibition of the parasite orthologue TcCLK1 in a recombinant enzyme assay.

The aminothiazoles were not clean. The best compound was moderately cytotoxic to primary cardiomyocytes, a real concern for a disease whose main complication is cardiac. Still, it cured four of six mice in a bioluminescent chronic-infection model when given for 20 days, and cyclophosphamide immunosuppression after treatment did not reveal relapse in those animals.

We think washout assays should become routine in Chagas screening cascades. They are slower and lower throughput, but they remove a large number of compounds that would otherwise fail later and at much greater cost.

The COVID-19 pandemic highlighted both the potential and the limitations of drug repurposing as a rapid response strategy to emerging viral threats. Dengue virus, which causes an estimated 390 million infections per year and for which no approved antiviral therapy exists, represents an important target for similar approaches. In the present study, we combined computational prioritisation with cell-based validation to identify approved or late-stage clinical compounds with activity against all four dengue virus serotypes.

First, we constructed a ranking pipeline integrating three sources of evidence: structure-based docking against the NS2B-NS3 protease and the NS5 RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, ligand-based similarity to compounds with reported anti-flavivirus activity, and host-factor network proximity derived from published CRISPR screens. Application of this pipeline to 6,214 compounds from the Drug Repurposing Hub resulted in a prioritised list of 240 candidates. These were tested in Huh-7 cells infected with DENV-2 using a high-content immunofluorescence assay, and 31 compounds reduced infection by more than 70% at 10 µM without significant cytotoxicity.

Dose-response experiments confirmed sub-micromolar activity for seven compounds. Among them, the kinase inhibitor fostamatinib and the antifungal itraconazole showed broad activity against DENV-1 to DENV-4, with EC50 values ranging from 0.3 to 1.8 µM. Time-of-addition experiments indicated that itraconazole acts at a post-entry stage, consistent with disruption of oxysterol-binding protein-mediated lipid transport required for replication organelle formation. In primary human monocyte-derived macrophages, both compounds decreased viral RNA levels by approximately two orders of magnitude. However, comparison with reported human plasma concentrations suggests that only itraconazole is likely to reach therapeutic levels at approved doses.

Notably, the computational ranking improved the hit rate approximately fourfold compared with a random selection of the same library, and host-directed evidence contributed most to this enrichment. These results support further evaluation of itraconazole in a dengue mouse model and demonstrate that integrating host and pathogen information can make repurposing screens more efficient, especially in settings where experimental resources are limited.

The increasing availability of machine learning models for molecular property prediction has created significant opportunities for drug discovery, particularly in resource-limited settings where experimental capacity is constrained. However, many published models remain difficult to use in practice due to inconsistent software dependencies, undocumented preprocessing steps and the absence of standardised interfaces. To address these challenges, we present ChemHarbor, an open-source, community-driven platform for the deployment and reuse of pretrained cheminformatics models.

ChemHarbor packages each model as a self-contained, versioned container with a uniform input and output schema, enabling users to run predictions with a single command irrespective of the underlying framework. At the time of writing, the platform hosts 187 models covering bioactivity against infectious disease targets, ADMET endpoints, physicochemical properties, molecular featurisation and generative tasks. Each model is accompanied by structured metadata describing its training data, intended use, evaluation metrics and known limitations, and is subjected to automated testing to verify reproducibility of the original authors' published outputs.

We evaluated the platform from three perspectives. First, a technical audit showed that 94% of incorporated models reproduced reported example outputs to within numerical tolerance, while the remaining 6% revealed discrepancies that were subsequently traced to undocumented preprocessing in the source code. Second, a benchmark of computational performance demonstrated that batch inference on 100,000 molecules could be completed on a standard laptop for the majority of models in under one hour. Third, a user study involving 42 researchers from 11 institutions in Africa, Latin America and Europe indicated that participants without prior programming experience were able to complete a virtual screening task with minimal guidance.

ChemHarbor lowers the technical barriers to applying state-of-the-art predictive models and promotes transparency and reproducibility in computational drug discovery. By emphasising openness, careful documentation and community contribution, the platform aims to support a more equitable distribution of computational tools across the global research community. The software is freely available under a GPLv3 licence, and we welcome contributions of new models from the wider scientific community.

Training programmes in computational drug discovery for African researchers have multiplied over the past decade, but almost none have been evaluated beyond end-of-course satisfaction forms. We followed up the participants of a twelve-week, part-online fellowship run between 2021 and 2024 to find out what, if anything, they did with the skills afterwards.

The fellowship enrolled 96 early-career scientists from 17 countries, mostly pharmacists, chemists and biologists with little or no programming background. It combined weekly remote sessions on Python, cheminformatics and model evaluation with a one-week in-person workshop and a mentored project built around the fellow's own research question. We surveyed fellows at completion, at 12 months and at 24 months, and interviewed a purposive subsample of 23 of them. We also tracked publications, preprints, code repositories and grant applications that listed the fellowship or its tools.

Retention was better than we expected. Eighty-one fellows completed the programme, and 64 responded at 24 months. Of those, 41 reported using computational methods in their ongoing work at least monthly, and 19 had published or preprinted a paper that included an analysis begun during the fellowship. Fewer had gone further: only seven had trained a model of their own on new data, and only four had secured funding that explicitly covered computational work.

The interviews were more telling than the numbers. Fellows described unreliable power and internet as a nuisance but not the main obstacle. What stopped them was isolation. Many were the only person in their department who could run the code, had no one to ask when something broke, and found that supervisors did not see computational work as real research. The fellows who kept going tended to have found a peer group, often through the programme's own messaging channel, or a senior colleague willing to protect their time.

Short courses can teach people to run tools. Sustaining their use needs institutional recognition and a network to fall back on, and funders should budget for both rather than for more training cohorts alone.

Deep generative models have attracted considerable attention as a means to explore chemical space beyond the limits of existing compound libraries. However, most published studies evaluate generated molecules using distribution-level metrics such as validity, uniqueness and novelty, which provide limited information about whether the molecules are useful for a real drug discovery project. In this work, we evaluated the practical value of a chemical language model for the design of inhibitors of Leishmania donovani N-myristoyltransferase (LdNMT), an enzyme that has been genetically and chemically validated as a drug target.

We pretrained a SMILES-based transformer on 1.9 million drug-like molecules from ChEMBL and fine-tuned it on 1,140 compounds with reported NMT activity. Molecular generation was then steered by reinforcement learning using a multi-parameter reward that combined a predicted LdNMT pIC50, selectivity against human NMT1, synthetic accessibility and a set of medicinal chemistry filters. From 50,000 generated structures, 3,600 passed all filters, and these were clustered and inspected by two medicinal chemists, who selected 28 molecules for synthesis on the basis of novelty and feasibility.

Of the 28 compounds, 22 were successfully synthesised within the planned timeframe. Eleven inhibited LdNMT with an IC50 below 1 µM, and four showed better than tenfold selectivity over the human enzyme. The most promising compound, GEN-19, contains a pyrazole-sulfonamide core that is not present in the fine-tuning set, displayed an IC50 of 38 nM against LdNMT, and inhibited intracellular amastigotes in mouse peritoneal macrophages with an EC50 of 2.4 µM. A co-crystal structure with the Leishmania major orthologue confirmed the predicted binding mode in the peptide-binding pocket.

We also observed important limitations. The predictor used in the reward function overestimated potency for compounds far from the training data, and several generated molecules with very high predicted scores were inactive. In addition, the translation from enzyme potency to cellular activity remained weak, which is a common challenge for this target. Despite these limitations, our study shows that generative models, when combined with expert curation, can deliver chemically novel and experimentally confirmed hits for a neglected disease target.

Generative models for de novo molecular design have advanced rapidly over the past several years, evolving from early recurrent neural networks trained on SMILES strings to sophisticated architectures based on variational autoencoders, graph neural networks, transformers and, more recently, diffusion models operating directly in three-dimensional space. These approaches hold considerable promise for accelerating the early stages of drug discovery by proposing novel compounds that satisfy multiple design objectives simultaneously, such as target potency, selectivity, favourable pharmacokinetics and synthetic tractability.

Despite this progress, a substantial gap remains between the performance of generative models on computational benchmarks and their demonstrated impact in prospective drug discovery campaigns. Widely used benchmarks such as GuacaMol and MOSES primarily assess the ability of a model to reproduce the statistical properties of a reference dataset or to optimise simple, computable objectives. While these benchmarks have been valuable for comparing methods, they do not capture many of the considerations that determine whether a generated molecule is genuinely useful, including its synthesisability, its chemical stability, and the reliability of the predictive models used to score it.

A particularly important and often underappreciated challenge is the so-called oracle problem. In most goal-directed generation workflows, the generative model is optimised against one or more surrogate predictors, which are themselves machine learning models trained on limited data. As the generator explores regions of chemical space increasingly distant from the training data of these predictors, it may exploit their weaknesses, producing molecules with high predicted scores that are unlikely to be active in practice. This phenomenon, analogous to reward hacking in reinforcement learning, has been documented in several studies but remains insufficiently addressed in the literature.

Furthermore, the vast majority of generative modelling studies have focused on targets relevant to oncology, neuroscience and other therapeutic areas with substantial commercial investment. Comparatively little attention has been paid to infectious diseases that disproportionately affect low- and middle-income countries, where data are often sparse and experimental validation capacity is limited. In these settings, the efficient use of generative models could be especially impactful, but it also requires approaches that are robust to small datasets and that explicitly account for predictive uncertainty.

In this work, we address these challenges by developing an uncertainty-aware generative framework that constrains exploration to regions where surrogate predictions are reliable, and we evaluate its performance in a prospective campaign targeting Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

Our results add to a growing body of evidence that the PI4K inhibitors are among the most promising antimalarial classes to emerge from the last decade of phenotypic screening, but they also raise a few problems that are worth stating plainly.

The first is potency against liver stages. The pyrazolopyridines described here are highly active against blood-stage parasites, yet their activity against P. berghei liver schizonts was roughly an order of magnitude weaker than that reported for MMV390048. We do not fully understand why. Differences in hepatocyte permeability are one possibility, and our limited data on accumulation in HepG2 cells point in that direction, but we have not ruled out that the liver-stage enzyme is simply less sensitive in this chemical context. If the series is to be positioned for chemoprotection, this gap will need to be closed, and we suspect it will take more than incremental changes to lipophilicity.

The second concerns safety. Teratogenicity findings ended the clinical development of MMV390048, and it is not yet clear whether this is an on-target effect of PI4K inhibition in the host or a compound-specific liability. Our selectivity data against human PI4KIIIβ are encouraging, with a margin of more than 300-fold for compound 22, but margins measured on isolated enzymes have a way of shrinking in vivo. We would be cautious about claiming that this series has escaped the problem until embryofetal studies have been done.

Third, resistance. We were able to select resistant parasites in vitro at a frequency of about 10^-7, somewhat lower than for several other fast-acting classes but not low enough to be reassuring. Every resistant clone carried a point mutation in the ATP-binding region of PfPI4K, and two of these conferred cross-resistance to KDU691. That argues against pairing compounds from these chemotypes in any future combination.

None of this means the series should be abandoned. Its oral exposure in mice is good, it kills quickly, and the chemistry is short and cheap, which matters for a drug that would ultimately need to sell for well under a dollar per course. But the history of this target suggests that blood-stage potency is the easy part. The work that remains is less glamorous and will decide whether these compounds ever reach a patient.

Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is now recognised as one of the most serious threats to global health. A recent systematic analysis estimated that bacterial AMR was directly responsible for approximately 1.14 million deaths in 2021 and associated with nearly 4.7 million deaths, with the highest mortality rates observed in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia. Despite this burden, the availability of reliable surveillance data in these regions remains limited, and many national estimates are based on modelling assumptions rather than on direct laboratory observations.

Effective surveillance is essential for several reasons. At the clinical level, local susceptibility data guide empirical antibiotic prescribing, which is particularly important in settings where culture results are not routinely available. At the public health level, surveillance allows the early detection of emerging resistance mechanisms, such as carbapenemases or plasmid-mediated colistin resistance, and supports the evaluation of stewardship and infection control interventions. Finally, at the global level, high-quality data from under-represented regions are necessary to improve burden estimates and to direct investment where it is most needed.

The World Health Organization launched the Global Antimicrobial Resistance and Use Surveillance System (GLASS) in 2015 to standardise data collection and reporting across member states. Participation has increased steadily, and more than 120 countries are now enrolled. However, the quality and completeness of the reported data vary considerably. In many low- and middle-income countries, microbiology laboratories face shortages of trained personnel, consumables and quality assurance systems, and blood culture is performed for only a small fraction of patients with suspected sepsis. As a result, the isolates that reach surveillance systems are often biased towards tertiary hospitals and towards patients who have already failed initial treatment, which may overestimate resistance in the general population.

Genomic surveillance offers additional resolution by identifying resistance genes, mobile genetic elements and transmission clusters. The cost of whole-genome sequencing has decreased considerably, and portable platforms such as Oxford Nanopore have made sequencing feasible in laboratories without large infrastructure. Nevertheless, the integration of genomic data into routine surveillance remains challenging, mainly because of limited bioinformatics capacity and the absence of sustainable funding models.

In this context, the present study aimed to evaluate the feasibility of a hub-and-spoke model combining phenotypic testing in district hospitals with regional genomic confirmation in Tanzania and Malawi, and to describe the resistance patterns observed during its first two years of operation.

In this study, we described the optimisation of a novel series of 2-pyridyl-thiazole inhibitors of Mycobacterium tuberculosis, progressing from a modestly potent screening hit to a lead compound with sub-micromolar whole-cell activity, favourable in vitro ADME properties and demonstrable efficacy in an acute murine infection model. Several aspects of these findings merit further discussion.

First, the mechanism of action studies strongly implicate the cytochrome bcc-aa3 supercomplex, and more specifically the QcrB subunit, as the primary target of this series. Resistant mutants consistently harboured substitutions at threonine 313, a residue previously associated with resistance to telacebec and other QcrB inhibitors. While this provides confidence in the target assignment, it also raises important considerations. QcrB inhibitors are known to be bacteriostatic rather than bactericidal against M. tuberculosis under standard conditions, owing to the ability of the organism to reroute electron flow through the alternative cytochrome bd oxidase. Consistent with this, our lead compound displayed limited bactericidal activity in vitro, and its efficacy in vivo was more modest than its MIC might suggest.

Second, these observations suggest that the most promising path forward for this series may lie in combination therapy. Previous studies have demonstrated that simultaneous inhibition of QcrB and cytochrome bd results in rapid bactericidal activity, and that QcrB inhibitors can potentiate the activity of bedaquiline and other agents targeting oxidative phosphorylation. Evaluation of our lead compound in combination with cytochrome bd inhibitors, as well as with existing first-line and second-line drugs, will therefore be an important next step.

Third, it is worth noting that the structure-activity relationships observed in this series differ in several respects from those reported for imidazopyridine amides. In particular, the tolerance of polar substituents at the 4-position of the thiazole ring allowed us to reduce lipophilicity substantially without compromising potency, which in turn contributed to improved solubility and reduced plasma protein binding.

Several limitations of this study should be acknowledged. The in vivo evaluation was restricted to an acute infection model, which may not fully reflect efficacy against the heterogeneous bacterial populations present in chronic human disease. In addition, cross-resistance profiling was limited to a small panel of clinical isolates. Future work will address these limitations and assess the potential of this series as a component of novel treatment regimens.

Visceral leishmaniasis is fatal if left untreated, and the drugs we have are either toxic, expensive, hard to give, or some combination of the three. Pentavalent antimonials still require weeks of painful injections and have lost much of their efficacy in Bihar. Liposomal amphotericin B works well in South Asia, but it needs a cold chain and intravenous infusion, and its performance in East Africa has been disappointing. Miltefosine is oral, which is a real advantage, but it is teratogenic, has a long half-life that invites resistance, and relapse rates after treatment have crept up in India and Nepal. Paromomycin sits somewhere in the middle and is mostly used in combination.

So the case for new oral drugs is not hard to make. What is harder is finding them. Leishmania amastigotes live inside the phagolysosome of macrophages, which means a compound has to cross the host cell membrane, survive an acidic compartment, and then reach the parasite. Phenotypic screens against free-living promastigotes are cheap and fast, but their hits translate poorly; a large fraction lose activity entirely in the intracellular assay. Screens run directly against intracellular amastigotes are more predictive, but they are slow, noisy, and depend on primary macrophages or cell lines whose behaviour does not always match infected tissue.

The past ten years have nonetheless produced several clinical candidates, almost all of them from a small number of public-private consortia. Compounds from the oxaborole, nitroimidazole, proteasome inhibitor and CRK12 inhibitor classes have reached phase I or beyond. That is a far better position than the field was in a decade ago. It is also fragile. Most of these molecules share a narrow set of mechanisms, and several have been dropped for safety or exposure reasons that were not obvious until late.

We think part of the problem is that most screening collections were assembled for other purposes, and the chemical space they cover was never designed with intracellular protozoa in mind. In this paper we take a different route. Rather than screen more compounds, we asked which physicochemical properties distinguish compounds that reach intracellular amastigotes from those that do not, using data from about 1.2 million compounds tested by three groups over fifteen years, and whether that knowledge can be used to build a better-targeted library.

In the present study, we developed and validated a set of machine learning models for the prediction of human liver microsomal stability, Caco-2 permeability and plasma protein binding, and we evaluated how their predictive performance changes when the models are applied to compounds from an academic antimalarial programme rather than to compounds similar to the training data. The main finding is that model accuracy decreased substantially for compounds outside the applicability domain, but that this decrease could be anticipated reasonably well using simple distance-based measures.

These results are in agreement with previous reports showing that the performance of ADMET models is strongly dependent on the similarity between training and query compounds. Most public ADMET datasets are dominated by compounds from pharmaceutical companies, which tend to occupy regions of chemical space optimised for oral drugs in therapeutic areas such as cardiovascular disease and oncology. In contrast, compounds from neglected disease programmes frequently present higher polarity, more heteroatoms and scaffolds that are uncommon in industrial libraries. In our analysis, nearly 40% of the antimalarial compounds had a maximum Tanimoto similarity below 0.4 to any compound in the training set, and for these compounds the root mean square error for microsomal clearance was approximately twice that observed in cross-validation.

An important practical consequence is that predictions for novel chemotypes should be interpreted with caution and accompanied by an estimate of reliability. We found that conformal prediction intervals were well calibrated in the random split but became too narrow for distant compounds, which suggests that standard calibration procedures may give a false sense of confidence. Combining conformal prediction with a nearest-neighbour distance threshold improved the identification of unreliable predictions, and we recommend this approach for users who apply these models to new chemical series.

We also observed that the addition of a relatively small number of in-house measurements, around 150 compounds, improved performance on the antimalarial set considerably, in particular for permeability. This indicates that local fine-tuning may be more valuable than increasing the size of the general training set, an observation that is relevant for academic groups with limited experimental budgets.

This study has some limitations. The external dataset came from a single programme, and the assays were performed in one laboratory, so inter-laboratory variability was not considered. In addition, we did not evaluate more recent foundation models, which may present different generalisation behaviour.

The emergence of SARS-CoV-2 in late 2019 prompted an unprecedented global effort to identify existing drugs that could be rapidly repurposed for the treatment of COVID-19. Drug repurposing offers several potential advantages over de novo drug development, including established safety profiles, known pharmacokinetic properties, existing manufacturing capacity and, consequently, substantially reduced development timelines and costs. These advantages are particularly relevant in the context of emerging infectious diseases, where the speed of response can have a decisive influence on public health outcomes.

During the pandemic, hundreds of approved drugs were proposed as potential COVID-19 therapeutics on the basis of in silico screening, in vitro antiviral assays or mechanistic hypotheses. However, the vast majority of these candidates failed to demonstrate clinical benefit in randomised controlled trials. Prominent examples include hydroxychloroquine, lopinavir-ritonavir and ivermectin, each of which attracted considerable attention before being shown to be ineffective in large clinical studies. Retrospective analyses have identified several factors that contributed to these failures, including the use of cell lines with limited physiological relevance, the testing of compounds at concentrations unachievable in human plasma or lung tissue, and the misinterpretation of nonspecific effects such as phospholipidosis as genuine antiviral activity.

These experiences offer valuable lessons for future repurposing efforts. In particular, they highlight the importance of considering pharmacokinetic feasibility early in the prioritisation process, of employing physiologically relevant cellular models such as primary airway epithelial cultures, and of implementing counter-screens to exclude compounds acting through nonspecific mechanisms. They also underscore the need for well-designed clinical trials capable of providing timely and definitive answers.

At the same time, the pandemic demonstrated that repurposing can succeed when these principles are followed. Dexamethasone and baricitinib, both identified through mechanistically grounded hypotheses regarding the host inflammatory response, were shown to reduce mortality in hospitalised patients and were rapidly incorporated into treatment guidelines worldwide.

Building on these lessons, the present study aims to establish a systematic and pharmacologically informed framework for antiviral repurposing that can be deployed rapidly in response to future outbreaks. We apply this framework retrospectively to SARS-CoV-2 and prospectively to Nipah virus, a priority pathogen for which no approved therapeutics currently exist.

When we started this programme in 2019, the idea that a small university laboratory in Cameroon could contribute original computational work to a drug discovery consortium was met with polite scepticism, including, at times, from us. Five years later, the group has published eleven papers, three of them as last author, has built two predictive models now used by partners in Europe and South Africa, and has trained twenty-seven students, most of whom are still doing research. It is worth reflecting on what made this possible, and what did not work.

The most useful decision was also the least exciting. We started with infrastructure that could survive local conditions rather than infrastructure that was fashionable. A modest cluster with battery backup and solar charging turned out to matter more than access to cloud credits, which were generous but unusable during the frequent periods when the university connection dropped below a few hundred kilobits per second. Tools that ran offline, on ordinary laptops, were adopted. Tools that needed a stable connection or a GPU were mostly not.

Second, the projects had to belong to the group. Early on, partners would send datasets and ask for a model, and the work felt like outsourced labour; motivation fell quickly and nothing was published locally. Things improved once students framed their own questions, often about plants used in local medicine or about pathogens they had seen in clinics, and partners supplied advice and compute rather than direction.

Not everything worked. A planned exchange programme stalled because visa refusals for two students were never explained, and we lost almost a year. Funding for salaries, as opposed to equipment and travel, remained almost impossible to find, and two of the most capable people left for better-paid jobs outside science. We do not have a solution to this, and we suspect no amount of training will compensate for it.

The broader lesson, we think, is that capacity building is mostly a question of time and ownership. Short workshops create interest. They rarely create a research group. That takes years of steady, unglamorous support, and funders who are prepared to stay the course long after the first round of publications.

Open-source software has become an essential component of modern cheminformatics and computational drug discovery. Libraries such as RDKit, Open Babel and the Chemistry Development Kit provide fundamental functionality for reading, manipulating and analysing chemical structures, and they are used by academic groups, pharmaceutical companies and startups alike. More recently, frameworks such as DeepChem, Chemprop and TorchDrug have made it considerably easier to train and apply machine learning models to molecular data, contributing to the rapid growth of the field.

Despite this progress, the reuse of published predictive models remains surprisingly difficult. Several surveys have shown that only a minority of machine learning papers in chemistry provide code that can be executed without modification, and an even smaller fraction provide trained model weights. In many cases, dependencies are not pinned to specific versions, preprocessing steps are described only in the text, and example input and output files are missing. As a consequence, researchers who wish to apply a published model to their own compounds frequently need to reimplement it, which requires expertise and time that are not always available.

This problem is especially significant for researchers in low- and middle-income countries. These researchers often work on diseases that receive limited attention from industry, such as malaria, tuberculosis and neglected tropical diseases, and could benefit greatly from computational tools that help to prioritise compounds before costly experiments. However, they also tend to have less access to dedicated computational staff, high-performance computing facilities and stable internet connections. Under these conditions, the difference between a model that can be installed with one command and a model that requires several days of troubleshooting is often the difference between using it and not using it.

Several initiatives have attempted to address this gap. Model repositories such as Hugging Face host a growing number of chemistry models, but they do not enforce a common input format or provide domain-specific metadata. Web servers offer easy access but generally cannot be run locally, which raises concerns about data confidentiality and long-term availability. Containerisation approaches improve reproducibility but are frequently considered too complex by non-specialist users.

In this article, we describe an approach that tries to combine the advantages of these strategies, and we report our experience from four years of maintaining a curated collection of ready-to-use models for infectious disease research.

The manuscript entitled "Graph attention networks enable accurate prediction of antiplasmodial activity across diverse chemical scaffolds" describes the development of a graph neural network model trained on publicly available data from ChEMBL and the MMV Malaria Box to predict inhibition of Plasmodium falciparum asexual blood-stage growth. The authors report an AUROC of 0.91 on a held-out test set and apply the model to virtually screen a commercial library of 1.2 million compounds, of which 40 were purchased and 9 confirmed as active in vitro. The topic is relevant and timely, and the manuscript is generally well written. However, several methodological concerns need to be addressed before the work can be considered for publication.

The main strength of the study lies in its prospective experimental validation, which is still relatively uncommon in this field and provides valuable evidence of practical utility. The authors are also commended for making their code available and for providing a clear description of the model architecture.

My most significant concern relates to the evaluation strategy. The test set appears to have been generated by random splitting, which is known to substantially overestimate performance when structurally similar compounds are present in both training and test sets. Given that the training data include large congeneric series from the GSK Tres Cantos and Novartis datasets, I would strongly encourage the authors to repeat the evaluation using a scaffold-based or cluster-based split and to report how performance changes. It would also be helpful to compare the model against simpler baselines, such as a random forest trained on Morgan fingerprints, as it is currently unclear whether the added complexity of the graph attention architecture provides a meaningful benefit.

A second concern is the definition of activity. The authors use a threshold of 10 µM to binarise the data, but the original assays differ in strain, readout and incubation time. A more detailed discussion of how these sources of heterogeneity were handled is needed.

Regarding the prospective validation, the hit rate of 22.5% is encouraging, but the authors should report the similarity of the confirmed hits to the nearest training compounds. If the actives are close analogues of known antimalarials, the claim of novel scaffold discovery would need to be tempered.

Minor points include the absence of confidence intervals for the reported metrics, inconsistent units in the second supplementary table, and several typographical errors in the Methods section. Overall, I recommend major revision.

This paper reports a two-year surveillance study of extended-spectrum beta-lactamase and carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales in five hospitals in northern Nigeria, combining routine susceptibility testing with short-read sequencing of 340 isolates. The authors describe high rates of third-generation cephalosporin resistance, a smaller but rising proportion of carbapenem resistance driven largely by blaNDM-5, and evidence of inter-hospital transmission of an ST147 Klebsiella clone. These are useful data from a region that is badly under-represented in the literature, and I think the paper should eventually be published. In its current form, though, it overstates what the sampling design can support.

My central concern is representativeness. The isolates come from specimens that clinicians chose to send for culture, and the Methods say little about how that decision was made. In most settings like this, cultures are sent after empirical treatment has failed, which enriches for resistant organisms. The headline prevalence figures in the abstract are therefore likely to be inflated if read as estimates of resistance in the hospital population, and the paper currently invites exactly that reading. I would ask the authors to report what fraction of admissions with suspected infection had a culture taken, to describe prior antibiotic exposure where it is recorded, and to reframe the prevalence estimates accordingly.

The transmission analysis is the most interesting part of the paper and also the thinnest. Pairwise SNP distances alone are not enough to infer hospital-to-hospital spread, particularly for a globally successful clone like ST147. Were patient transfers documented? Is there any epidemiological link between the clustered cases? Without this, I would describe the clusters as consistent with transmission rather than demonstrating it.

I was also unsure how the sequenced subset was chosen. The text says isolates were selected "to represent the diversity of resistance phenotypes", which could mean several things, and the choice affects every downstream frequency estimate.

Smaller points. The breakpoints used should be stated explicitly, with the CLSI or EUCAST version. The phylogeny figure is hard to read in print; collapsing well-supported clades would help. Several sentences in the Discussion repeat the Results almost verbatim and could go. Finally, the authors mention that sequence data have been deposited, but I could not find accession numbers.

None of these issues is fatal. Most can be fixed by being more careful about what the data show. Major revision.

In this manuscript, the authors present the hit-to-lead optimisation of a series of 2-aminoquinazolines with activity against Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Starting from a screening hit with an MIC of 6.2 µM, they synthesised 64 analogues, identified a lead compound with an MIC of 0.2 µM and reasonable microsomal stability, and propose DprE1 as the molecular target on the basis of resistant mutant sequencing. The work is clearly within the scope of the journal and addresses an important need. The chemistry is described in sufficient detail, and the compound characterisation appears to be of good quality. Nevertheless, I have several concerns regarding the biological evaluation and the interpretation of the results.

First, the target assignment requires additional support. The authors report that two resistant mutants carry mutations in dprE1, but they do not show enzymatic inhibition data with purified DprE1, nor do they test the lead compound against strains overexpressing the enzyme. Since several published DprE1 inhibitors are covalent and depend on a nitro group, which is absent in this series, I believe the authors should at least provide biochemical inhibition data and discuss whether the mode of binding is likely to be covalent or non-covalent.

Second, the selectivity and safety profile is not sufficiently characterised. Cytotoxicity was measured only in Vero cells, and the selectivity index of the lead compound is approximately 25, which is modest. I recommend testing in at least one additional human cell line such as HepG2 and, considering the planar aromatic structure of the series, including an assessment of hERG inhibition.

Third, the structure-activity relationship discussion would benefit from a more quantitative presentation. At the moment, the trends are described qualitatively, and it is difficult for the reader to follow which modifications produced the main improvements. A summary figure or a matched molecular pair analysis would make the conclusions clearer.

Fourth, the claim in the Abstract that the lead compound is "suitable for in vivo studies" seems premature. Plasma protein binding, solubility and pharmacokinetic data are not reported, and the mouse microsomal half-life of 18 minutes suggests that exposure may be limited.

Minor comments: the MIC determination method should specify the medium and whether Tween 80 was used; some compound numbers in the second table do not match the text; and the reference list contains duplicated entries.

In summary, the study is promising, but I recommend major revision before it can be accepted.

This manuscript presents a comparative evaluation of transformer-based chemical language models for the prediction of ADMET properties, using the Therapeutics Data Commons benchmark suite as the primary evaluation framework. The authors fine-tune four publicly available pretrained models on 22 ADMET tasks and compare their performance with established baselines, including Chemprop and gradient-boosted trees trained on molecular fingerprints. They conclude that chemical language models achieve state-of-the-art performance on the majority of tasks and recommend their adoption as a default approach for ADMET modelling.

The study addresses a question of considerable practical importance, as the choice of modelling approach for ADMET prediction has direct implications for compound prioritisation in drug discovery projects. The manuscript is well organised, the figures are clear and informative, and the authors have made their fine-tuning code publicly available, which is commendable.

However, I have a number of substantive concerns regarding the experimental design and the strength of the conclusions. Most importantly, the reported improvements over baselines are frequently small and fall within the range of variation observed across random seeds. The authors report mean performance over three seeds but do not present any formal statistical comparison. Given the number of tasks and models being compared, I would recommend the use of an appropriate statistical test with correction for multiple comparisons, or at minimum the reporting of standard deviations alongside all summary statistics.

Additionally, the hyperparameter optimisation procedure appears to differ substantially between the language models and the baselines. The language models were tuned using an extensive grid search, whereas the baselines appear to have been run with default settings. This asymmetry could account for a considerable portion of the observed performance differences and should be addressed to ensure a fair comparison.

I also note that the computational cost of each approach is not discussed. Given that fine-tuning large language models requires significantly greater resources than training tree-based models, a discussion of the trade-off between performance and computational expense would be valuable, particularly for readers working in resource-constrained environments.

Finally, the recommendation that chemical language models should be adopted as a default approach appears overstated in light of the evidence presented and should be moderated accordingly.

Minor points: several tasks in the supplementary tables lack units; the description of the scaffold split should be expanded; and the term "state-of-the-art" is used inconsistently throughout the text. I recommend major revision.

The authors set out to identify new starting points for schistosomiasis by screening 1,800 compounds from a natural product-derived library against Schistosoma mansoni newly transformed schistosomula and adult worms. They report 14 hits active against both stages, follow up three of them with dose-response and motility assays, and show that one, a modified sesquiterpene lactone, reduces worm burden by 58% in infected mice after a single oral dose of 400 mg/kg. The main argument is that this compound is a viable alternative to praziquantel, particularly because it retains activity against juvenile worms.

I liked several things about the paper. Schistosomiasis badly needs alternatives to praziquantel, and activity against juvenile stages is exactly where praziquantel is weak. The screening is careful, the imaging-based phenotypic scoring is well described, and the authors are honest about the limited activity of most hits.

The in vivo result, though, does not carry the weight placed on it. A 58% reduction in worm burden at 400 mg/kg is a modest effect at a very high dose. For comparison, praziquantel at the same dose in this model typically gives reductions above 90%. I do not think the data justify the phrase "viable alternative", and the abstract and title should be revised. It would also help to know whether female worms and egg burden were affected differently, since egg-induced pathology is what drives disease.

The selectivity data are thin. Cytotoxicity was measured in a single cell line at a single time point, and sesquiterpene lactones are reactive Michael acceptors with a long history of promiscuous activity. Some evidence that the antischistosomal effect is not simply general thiol reactivity would be valuable, for example by testing a saturated analogue lacking the alpha-methylene group.

I would also like to see the pharmacokinetic data, even if limited. Without any exposure measurements it is hard to interpret either the efficacy or the lack of it.

Smaller issues: the hit criteria differ between the two stages and the reasons are not explained; the motility scoring scale should be defined in the main text rather than the supplement; and the dose-response figure would be easier to read with consistent axes.

This is useful work and a reasonable starting point. It is not yet a candidate. Major revision.

The submitted manuscript describes a computational repurposing study aimed at identifying approved drugs with potential activity against Mpox virus. The authors performed molecular docking of 2,560 approved drugs against five viral proteins, including the F13 envelope protein and the DNA polymerase, followed by 200-nanosecond molecular dynamics simulations and MM-GBSA free energy calculations for the top 20 compounds per target. They propose eight drugs, including several antibiotics and antihistamines, as promising candidates for experimental evaluation.

The topic is relevant, considering the recent outbreaks and the limited therapeutic options for Mpox. The computational workflow is described in detail, and the simulation protocols follow generally accepted practices. However, I have serious concerns about the validity of the main conclusions, and I believe that the manuscript, in its present form, does not provide sufficient evidence to support the claims made.

My principal concern is the absence of any experimental validation. Docking scores and MM-GBSA energies are known to correlate poorly with measured binding affinities, especially when comparing chemically diverse compounds, and the false positive rate of virtual screening campaigns without experimental follow-up is very high. I understand that experimental work with Mpox requires biosafety facilities that may not be available to the authors, but at minimum the conclusions should be formulated much more cautiously, and the term "potential inhibitors" should be clearly distinguished from confirmed activity.

Second, the workflow lacks positive and negative controls. The authors should demonstrate that their docking protocol can recover tecovirimat, which is known to bind F13, and that it can discriminate known actives from decoys, for example by reporting enrichment factors. Without such validation, it is difficult to judge whether the rankings are meaningful.

Third, the structural models used for several proteins were obtained from AlphaFold predictions, but the confidence of these predictions in the binding regions is not reported. For a homology or predicted model, local pLDDT values in the pocket should be presented.

Fourth, the pharmacological plausibility of the candidates is not discussed. Several proposed drugs reach plasma concentrations in the low nanomolar range, which would make antiviral activity unlikely even if binding occurred.

Minor issues include inconsistent naming of the viral proteins, missing details on protonation state assignment, and figures with low resolution. Because of these concerns, I recommend rejection in the current form, with encouragement to resubmit after including validation.

This manuscript describes an open-source Python package designed to standardise the curation of bioactivity data for machine learning applications in drug discovery. The software provides modules for chemical structure standardisation, handling of stereochemistry and tautomers, aggregation of replicate measurements, detection of activity cliffs and generation of train-test splits according to several established strategies. The authors demonstrate the utility of the package by applying it to 40 ChEMBL target datasets and show that models trained on curated data exhibit improved and more consistent performance compared to those trained on uncurated data.

The package addresses a genuine and widely recognised need in the community. Data curation is frequently performed in an ad hoc manner, and inconsistencies in curation procedures are an important but underappreciated source of irreproducibility in published machine learning studies. The authors are to be commended for developing a well-documented tool with a clean interface, comprehensive unit tests and continuous integration. I was able to install the package and reproduce the main example from the documentation without difficulty.

Nevertheless, there are several aspects of the manuscript that could be improved. First, the comparison with existing tools is limited. Several packages, including the ChEMBL structure pipeline, MolVS and datamol, already provide overlapping functionality. The authors should more clearly articulate the specific advantages of their tool relative to these alternatives, ideally through a feature comparison table and a direct benchmark on a shared task.

Second, the evaluation of the impact of curation on model performance would benefit from additional rigour. The improvements reported appear to be modest for many targets, and it is not clear which curation steps contribute most to the observed gains. An ablation analysis isolating the effect of each step would considerably strengthen the manuscript and provide useful guidance to users.

Third, some default parameter choices, such as the threshold for removing measurements with high variance across replicates, are not justified. Since many users will rely on defaults, a discussion of how these were selected and how sensitive results are to them would be valuable.

Minor points: the manuscript would benefit from a short section describing the long-term maintenance plan for the software; the licence should be stated in the main text; and a few figure legends lack sufficient detail to be interpreted independently.

Overall, this is a useful contribution, and I recommend minor revision.

The manuscript reports on a capacity-building initiative that trained 120 researchers from 14 African countries in the use of computational tools for drug discovery between 2022 and 2024. The authors describe the curriculum, the delivery format, which mixed online modules with regional in-person workshops, and an evaluation based on pre- and post-training knowledge tests, participant satisfaction surveys, and a count of subsequent publications. They conclude that the programme substantially increased computational capacity among participants and propose it as a model for similar initiatives.

I want to say first that this is the kind of work that deserves to be published. Programmes like this are common, and they are almost never written up in enough detail for others to learn from. The curriculum description is genuinely useful, and the frank account of what went wrong with the first online cohort, where completion fell below 40%, was one of the more valuable parts of the paper.

My main concern is that the evaluation does not support the strength of the conclusions. Knowledge test scores improved, which is expected immediately after a course, but there is no longer-term follow-up of whether participants kept using what they learned. Satisfaction surveys tell us people enjoyed the training, not that it built capacity. The publication count is the closest thing to an outcome measure, yet the paper does not say how many of these publications would plausibly have happened anyway, or what role the training played in them. I would suggest the authors either collect follow-up data, even from a subsample, or rephrase the conclusions to describe what was delivered and what participants reported, rather than what capacity was created.

Related to this, the selection of participants needs more description. If applicants were chosen partly on prior experience, the most motivated and best-resourced researchers will have been favoured, which matters for any claims about transferability.

There is very little in the paper about institutions. Several participants are quoted as saying that they had no time or support to apply the skills on returning home. That seems to me the most important finding, and it deserves more than a sentence in the Discussion.

Minor points. The term "capacity" is used loosely and would benefit from a working definition early on. Some tables report percentages without denominators. The cost per participant would be very helpful to funders and is not given.

Minor to major revision, depending on whether follow-up data can be added.

This study proposes a new conditional diffusion model for the generation of three-dimensional molecules within protein binding pockets, and applies it to the design of inhibitors for the Trypanosoma brucei enzyme trypanothione reductase. The authors compare their method with three published structure-based generative models on the CrossDocked benchmark and report improvements in Vina docking scores, validity and diversity. In addition, they select ten generated molecules, perform molecular dynamics simulations, and suggest that several of them are promising candidates for further development.

The methodological contribution is interesting. The proposed equivariant architecture that conditions on both pocket geometry and pharmacophore features is well motivated, and the paper is generally well written with clear mathematical notation. Application to a neglected disease target is also welcome, since most work in this area focuses on well-studied human proteins.

However, I have important reservations concerning the evaluation. The main metric used to claim superiority is the Vina docking score of generated molecules. It is now well documented that generative models can produce molecules with favourable docking scores that are chemically unrealistic, for example structures with strained ring systems, unusual tautomers or excessive molecular weight. I would ask the authors to report, in addition to docking scores, the distribution of molecular weight, number of rotatable bonds, strain energy after relaxation, and the fraction of molecules passing standard medicinal chemistry filters. A comparison of these properties with those of known ligands of the targets in the benchmark would also be informative.

Second, the evaluation on trypanothione reductase is not convincing in its current form. The binding site of this enzyme is large, hydrophobic and known to be difficult to target with drug-like molecules. Without any experimental validation, the claim that the generated molecules are "promising inhibitors" is not supported. I recommend either including experimental data or clearly presenting this section as an illustrative case study.

Third, the synthetic accessibility of the generated molecules is reported only through the SA score, which is a rough heuristic. A retrosynthetic analysis for the selected compounds would greatly increase confidence.

Minor points: the training and test split of CrossDocked should be explicitly described to exclude data leakage; the computational cost of sampling relative to the baselines should be reported; and some abbreviations are not defined at first use.

I recommend major revision.

The overall objective of this proposal is to identify and characterise novel inhibitors of Plasmodium falciparum with the potential to block transmission of malaria from humans to mosquitoes. Current antimalarial therapies are primarily directed against the asexual blood stages responsible for clinical disease, but most have limited activity against mature stage V gametocytes, the parasite forms responsible for transmission. As malaria elimination efforts intensify across sub-Saharan Africa, there is a pressing need for compounds that can interrupt the transmission cycle and thereby reduce the spread of drug-resistant parasites. To address this need, we propose the following three specific aims.

Specific Aim 1: To develop and validate a machine learning model for predicting gametocytocidal activity. We will assemble a comprehensive dataset of approximately 25,000 compounds with published activity against late-stage gametocytes, together with associated asexual blood-stage data. Using this dataset, we will train and rigorously evaluate predictive models based on multiple molecular representations, applying scaffold-based splits and uncertainty quantification to ensure reliable performance on novel chemistry. We hypothesise that integrating asexual stage activity as an auxiliary task will improve predictive performance for the data-limited gametocyte endpoint.

Specific Aim 2: To prioritise and experimentally evaluate candidate transmission-blocking compounds. We will apply the models developed in Aim 1 to screen a virtual library of 3.5 million commercially available compounds, selecting approximately 400 candidates for experimental testing. Compounds will be evaluated in a luciferase-based stage V gametocyte viability assay and confirmed in the standard membrane feeding assay using Anopheles stephensi mosquitoes. We anticipate identifying at least 15 novel chemotypes with confirmed transmission-blocking activity.

Specific Aim 3: To characterise the mode of action and early developability of prioritised hits. For the most promising series, we will conduct in vitro resistance selection, chemical proteomics and metabolomic profiling to elucidate their mechanisms of action. In parallel, key ADMET properties, including solubility, metabolic stability and cytotoxicity, will be assessed to inform subsequent optimisation.

Upon successful completion of this project, we expect to deliver a validated, openly available predictive model for gametocytocidal activity, a set of experimentally confirmed transmission-blocking chemotypes with preliminary mechanistic annotation, and a framework that can be extended to other parasite life-cycle stages. These outcomes will provide a strong foundation for future hit-to-lead efforts and contribute to global malaria elimination goals.

Most hospitals in Uganda prescribe antibiotics for suspected sepsis without knowing what they are treating. Blood cultures are taken in a minority of cases, results take a week if they come back at all, and national resistance data are drawn largely from two referral laboratories in Kampala. Clinicians in district hospitals are left to guess, and they guess conservatively, which in practice means ceftriaxone for almost everyone. We think this gap between what is known about resistance and what reaches the ward is now one of the main drivers of poor outcomes in neonatal and adult sepsis, and that it can be narrowed without waiting for full laboratory infrastructure to arrive.

This project builds on three years of pilot work in four districts in western Uganda. During the pilot, we introduced a simplified blood culture workflow using automated incubators and a reduced panel of disc diffusion tests, supported by remote image-based quality control from a regional hub. Culture rates in febrile admissions rose from 6% to 31%. Turnaround from collection to a susceptibility result on the ward fell to a median of three days. Perhaps more importantly, the data were trusted. Two of the four hospitals changed their empirical sepsis guidance during the pilot, and one stopped using ceftriaxone as first-line therapy in neonates altogether.

What we cannot yet say is whether this changes what happens to patients. The pilot was not designed to measure mortality, and it is entirely possible that faster data alter prescribing without altering survival, particularly where second-line drugs are frequently out of stock. That is the question this proposal addresses.

We will run a stepped-wedge cluster trial across 16 district hospitals, introducing the workflow in four waves over 30 months. The primary outcome is 28-day mortality in patients admitted with suspected sepsis. Secondary outcomes include time to appropriate therapy, antibiotic use, and cost per patient. A nested qualitative study will look at how clinicians actually use, ignore or misread the reports, since that is where similar interventions have tended to fail.

If the approach works, it is cheap enough to scale. The Ministry of Health has agreed to consider it for the next national AMR action plan, and that is the route by which we expect the results to matter.

Tuberculosis remains a major public health problem in Ethiopia, which is listed by the World Health Organization among the 30 countries with the highest burden of tuberculosis and of TB/HIV co-infection. Treatment of drug-susceptible disease still requires six months of combination therapy, and multidrug-resistant tuberculosis requires longer, more toxic and more expensive regimens. New drugs with novel mechanisms of action are therefore urgently needed. At the same time, the capacity to perform early-stage drug discovery in Ethiopia, and in East Africa more generally, is very limited, and most chemical starting points for tuberculosis come from screening campaigns conducted in Europe and North America.

The significance of this proposal is twofold. Scientifically, we aim to progress a promising series of 4-aminoquinoline-3-carboxamides, identified in a previous collaborative screen, from hit to lead stage. The series shows sub-micromolar activity against Mycobacterium tuberculosis H37Rv, activity against several drug-resistant clinical isolates collected in Addis Ababa, and a mechanism of action that appears to be distinct from that of currently used drugs, based on preliminary transcriptional profiling. However, the current compounds present high lipophilicity and poor metabolic stability, which must be improved before in vivo evaluation can be considered. Through iterative design, synthesis and testing supported by computational models for potency and ADMET properties, we expect to deliver at least one lead compound meeting predefined criteria, including an MIC below 0.5 µM, a microsomal half-life above 30 minutes and a selectivity index above 100.

Second, the project has an important capacity-building dimension. All synthetic chemistry and whole-cell testing will be conducted at Addis Ababa University and the Armauer Hansen Research Institute, with computational and pharmacokinetic support provided by partners in South Africa and Spain. Two PhD students and one postdoctoral researcher will be trained in medicinal chemistry, mycobacterial assays and the use of open-source predictive tools. We consider this local ownership to be essential, because it ensures that the expertise generated remains in the country and can be applied to future projects on tuberculosis and other infectious diseases.

In addition, the project will contribute openly to the global research community. All compound structures and associated biological data will be deposited in public databases upon publication, and the predictive models developed will be made freely available. In this way, the results will benefit not only our consortium but also other groups working on tuberculosis drug discovery in resource-limited settings.

Aim 2 will focus on the development of robust and interpretable machine learning models for predicting key ADMET properties relevant to anti-infective drug discovery, with a specific emphasis on reliable performance for chemical series emerging from academic programmes in low- and middle-income countries.

Rationale. Existing ADMET prediction tools have been trained predominantly on data from pharmaceutical companies and are therefore biased towards chemical space associated with traditional therapeutic areas. Our preliminary analyses indicate that compounds from neglected disease programmes frequently fall outside the applicability domain of these models, resulting in substantially reduced predictive accuracy. In addition, most available tools provide point predictions without any indication of their reliability, which limits their usefulness for decision-making in projects with constrained experimental budgets.

Approach. We will first assemble a harmonised dataset covering eight priority endpoints: aqueous solubility, human and mouse liver microsomal stability, Caco-2 permeability, plasma protein binding, hERG inhibition, HepG2 cytotoxicity and CYP3A4 inhibition. Public data from ChEMBL and the Therapeutics Data Commons will be supplemented with approximately 12,000 previously unpublished measurements contributed by consortium partners working on malaria, tuberculosis and kinetoplastid diseases. All data will undergo rigorous curation, including structure standardisation, unit harmonisation and aggregation of replicate measurements.

Using this dataset, we will systematically compare a range of modelling strategies, including gradient-boosted trees, message-passing neural networks and fine-tuned pretrained chemical language models. Models will be evaluated using scaffold-based and time-based splits, as well as a dedicated external test set comprising compounds from partner programmes that are structurally distinct from the training data. Particular attention will be given to uncertainty quantification. We will implement conformal prediction and ensemble-based approaches and assess the calibration of the resulting uncertainty estimates as a function of distance from the training set.

To enhance interpretability, we will incorporate attribution methods that highlight substructures associated with predicted liabilities, enabling medicinal chemists to use model outputs to guide structural modifications.

Expected outcomes and potential pitfalls. We anticipate that this aim will produce a suite of openly available ADMET models with well-characterised applicability domains and calibrated uncertainty estimates. A potential challenge is the heterogeneity of experimental protocols across contributing laboratories. To mitigate this, we will record assay metadata in a standardised format and evaluate the impact of laboratory-specific effects on model performance.

Cutaneous leishmaniasis rarely kills anyone, which is one reason it gets so little attention. It does, however, leave scars that last for life, often on the face, and in parts of Syria, Afghanistan, Ethiopia and Peru those scars carry real social and economic costs, particularly for women and children. Treatment still relies on antimonials, given either by painful intralesional injection or by weeks of intramuscular dosing, and on thermotherapy where the equipment exists. There is no oral drug that works well across the main causative species, and the few candidates in development were mostly optimised for visceral disease.

Our aim is to find compounds that work in the skin. That sounds obvious, but it has practical consequences. Parasites in a cutaneous lesion sit in dermal macrophages surrounded by inflamed, sometimes necrotic tissue, and the drug exposure achieved there after oral dosing can be quite different from what is seen in plasma or liver.
