Several compounds with good activity in visceral models have been disappointing in cutaneous ones, and we suspect skin distribution explains much of this, although it has hardly been measured.

The project has three parts. First, we will screen around 15,000 compounds, drawn from open-access collections such as the MMV Pandemic Response Box and from our partners' kinetoplastid libraries, against intracellular amastigotes of L. major, L. tropica and L. braziliensis. Running three species in parallel costs more, but it avoids the familiar situation in which a promising compound turns out to be inactive against the species that matters in a given region. Second, for compounds active against all three, we will measure accumulation in an ex vivo human skin explant model developed in our laboratory, alongside standard ADME assays. Third, the best five to ten compounds will be tested in a BALB/c footpad model, with lesion tissue drug levels measured by LC-MS/MS at several time points.

We are realistic about what this can achieve in three years. We do not expect to deliver a clinical candidate. We do expect to hand over two or three well-characterised series with known skin exposure, and to publish the explant method and data so that others can stop guessing how much drug actually reaches the lesion.

The main objective of this project is to establish an integrated platform for the rapid identification of repurposable antiviral drugs against emerging arboviruses, with a focus on chikungunya, Zika and Oropouche viruses, which have caused repeated outbreaks in Brazil and in other countries of Latin America over the last decade. None of these viruses has an approved specific antiviral treatment, and the recent expansion of Oropouche virus to new regions has shown that our preparedness for such events remains insufficient.

To achieve this objective, we propose three specific aims.

Specific Aim 1 is to build a computational prioritisation pipeline that combines target-based and host-based evidence. For each virus, we will collect available structural information on viral proteins, including experimental structures and high-confidence predicted models, and perform docking of approximately 8,000 approved and clinical-stage compounds. In parallel, we will integrate published data on host factors required for viral replication, obtained from CRISPR and proteomic studies, and use network-based methods to identify drugs that act on these host factors. The two sources of evidence will be combined with pharmacokinetic information, so that compounds unlikely to reach effective concentrations in humans are deprioritised from the start.

Specific Aim 2 is to evaluate the prioritised compounds experimentally. Approximately 300 compounds will be tested in Vero and Huh-7 cells infected with each virus, using an automated immunofluorescence assay already established in our laboratory. Active compounds will be confirmed in dose-response experiments and evaluated in more physiologically relevant models, including primary human fibroblasts for chikungunya and neural progenitor cells for Zika. We expect to confirm at least ten compounds with broad or virus-specific activity at clinically achievable concentrations.

Specific Aim 3 is to test the most promising candidates in established mouse models of infection and to characterise their mechanism of action through time-of-addition assays and selection of resistant viruses. We plan to evaluate at least three compounds in vivo, either as monotherapy or in combination.

The expected outcome of this project is a validated set of repurposing candidates, together with an open and reusable pipeline that can be quickly applied to new arboviruses when they emerge. Importantly, all work will be performed in Brazil by a team with experience in both computational and experimental virology, which will strengthen national capacity for outbreak response and reduce the dependence on external partners during public health emergencies.

The significance of this project lies in its potential to substantially lower the barriers to the adoption of artificial intelligence in drug discovery research across sub-Saharan Africa. While the past decade has witnessed remarkable advances in machine learning methods for molecular property prediction, de novo design and virtual screening, the benefits of these advances have been unevenly distributed. Researchers in African institutions face a range of interconnected challenges, including limited access to computational infrastructure, unreliable internet connectivity, a shortage of specialised training opportunities and a scarcity of tools designed with their specific needs and research priorities in mind.

These challenges are particularly consequential because African researchers are uniquely positioned to address many of the infectious diseases that disproportionately affect the continent. Malaria, tuberculosis, HIV and neglected tropical diseases account for a substantial share of the disease burden in the region, yet the global drug discovery pipeline for these conditions remains underfunded and heavily dependent on research conducted elsewhere. Strengthening local capacity to apply computational methods would not only accelerate the discovery of new treatments but also ensure that research priorities are shaped by those most affected by these diseases.

This project will address these challenges through a comprehensive and integrated approach. First, we will develop and distribute a lightweight, offline-capable software platform that provides access to more than 150 pretrained models relevant to infectious disease drug discovery. The platform will be specifically optimised to run on standard laptops without requiring graphics processing units or continuous internet access. Second, we will establish a network of regional training hubs in Nigeria, Kenya, Ghana and South Africa, which will deliver structured training programmes and provide ongoing mentorship to participants. Third, we will support a cohort of 30 research fellows in applying these tools to their own research questions, with dedicated funding for experimental validation of computational predictions.

The anticipated impact of this project extends beyond the immediate outputs. By fostering a self-sustaining community of practice and embedding computational skills within African institutions, the project will contribute to a long-term shift in how drug discovery research is conducted on the continent. Moreover, the open-source nature of all software and training materials will enable their adaptation and reuse by other organisations and in other regions, thereby maximising the return on investment and contributing to a more equitable global research ecosystem.

Generative models can now propose molecules faster than any chemist can read them. The bottleneck has moved. What limits their use in neglected disease programmes is not the quality of the generator but the quality of the scoring functions it is optimised against, which are usually QSAR models trained on a few hundred measurements and trusted well beyond their range. Left unchecked, a generator will find the blind spots of the predictor and fill a shortlist with compounds that look excellent on paper and fail in the assay. We have seen this ourselves. In a pilot on Trypanosoma cruzi, 14 of the 16 top-ranked generated compounds we made were inactive, and nearly all of them sat far from the training data.

This proposal is about making generative design honest about what it does not know. Our approach rests on two ideas. The first is to restrict generation to regions of chemical space where the scoring model is reliable, using an applicability-domain penalty derived from ensemble disagreement and nearest-neighbour distance. The second is to treat the experiments themselves as part of the loop. Rather than generating a large batch once and testing the top, we will run small rounds of 20 to 30 compounds, retrain after each round, and allow the generator to explore further only when new data justify it.

We will test this on two targets where we already have chemistry and assays in place: T. cruzi CYP51 counter-selected against human CYP3A4, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis DprE1. For each, we will run the adaptive protocol in parallel with a conventional one-shot campaign of the same total size, so that the comparison is direct. Compounds will be sourced from make-on-demand libraries wherever possible, which keeps the cost per round under control and avoids the problem of designs that cannot be made.

Our success criterion is simple. Over five rounds, the adaptive arm should deliver at least twice as many confirmed actives below 1 µM as the conventional arm, and its actives should not be close analogues of the training set. If it does not, that is also worth knowing, and we will publish the negative result alongside the code.

The broader point is cultural as much as technical. Generative chemistry has been oversold, and groups with small budgets cannot afford to learn that the hard way.

Schistosomiasis affects more than 200 million people, the majority of them in sub-Saharan Africa, and its control depends almost entirely on a single drug, praziquantel. Mass drug administration with praziquantel has reduced morbidity in many endemic areas, but this strategy has important weaknesses. The drug has low activity against juvenile schistosomes, so reinfection and persistent transmission are common in high-burden communities. In addition, reduced cure rates have been reported in some foci in Senegal, Uganda and Egypt, and although true resistance has not been confirmed in the field, the reliance on one compound for hundreds of millions of treatments each year represents a serious risk for control programmes.

The approach of this project is based on a combination of computational prioritisation and phenotypic screening, performed in Côte d'Ivoire and in collaboration with partners in Switzerland and Spain. In the first work package, we will use a set of openly available machine learning models to screen approximately 600,000 commercially available compounds for predicted activity against Schistosoma mansoni, together with predicted solubility, permeability and cytotoxicity. These models were trained on public data from more than 9,000 compounds previously tested against schistosomula and adult worms. Because these data are limited and chemically heterogeneous, we will combine model scores with similarity to known antischistosomal chemotypes and with an estimate of prediction uncertainty, and we will select a diverse set of 1,000 compounds for purchase.

In the second work package, these compounds will be tested against newly transformed schistosomula using an automated imaging assay that measures changes in motility and morphology. Compounds showing activity at 10 µM will be evaluated against adult worms of both sexes and against juvenile liver-stage worms isolated from infected mice, since activity against juvenile stages is the property most needed to complement praziquantel. We expect a hit rate of about 3 to 5 percent, which is several times higher than that observed in previous random screens.

In the third work package, the experimental results will be used to retrain the models, and a second round of selection and testing will be performed. This iterative design will allow us to evaluate whether active learning can improve the efficiency of screening for neglected diseases where data are scarce.

All screening will be performed in our laboratory in Abidjan, and the resulting data and models will be released openly to support other research groups working on helminth diseases.

Malaria remains a major global health burden, and the emergence of artemisinin partial resistance in East Africa threatens the efficacy of current first-line therapies. There is an urgent need for new chemical matter with novel mechanisms of action that is active against both the asexual blood stages and the transmissible gametocyte stages of Plasmodium falciparum. Here, we report the discovery and optimization of a series of 2,4-diaminothienopyrimidines identified through a phenotypic screen of 18,400 compounds against the chloroquine-resistant Dd2 strain. The primary screen yielded 312 confirmed hits with EC50 values below 1 micromolar, of which 47 were prioritized based on selectivity over HepG2 cells and favorable physicochemical properties.

Structure-activity relationship studies on 138 analogues revealed that substitution at the C6 position with a basic amine side chain markedly improved both potency and aqueous solubility. The lead compound, designated TP-117, displayed an EC50 of 12 nanomolar against Dd2 and 21 nanomolar against the multidrug-resistant K1 strain, with a selectivity index greater than 400. TP-117 also inhibited late-stage gametocytes with an EC50 of 85 nanomolar and reduced oocyst formation by 94 percent in a standard membrane feeding assay. In vitro ADME profiling demonstrated moderate metabolic stability in human liver microsomes, with a half-life of 38 minutes, and low risk of CYP3A4 inhibition.

In the Plasmodium berghei mouse model, oral administration of TP-117 at 30 mg/kg once daily for four days resulted in a 99.2 percent reduction in parasitemia and extended mean survival beyond 30 days. Resistance selection experiments over 60 days did not yield stable resistant clones, although whole-genome sequencing of partially tolerant populations identified mutations in a putative amino acid transporter. Taken together, these results establish the thienopyrimidine scaffold as a promising starting point for multistage antimalarial development and provide a foundation for further optimization toward a single-dose cure. All screening data have been deposited in a public repository to support open and collaborative drug discovery efforts.

We wanted to know whether a machine learning model trained on public tuberculosis data could do something useful for a medicinal chemistry team that has only a few hundred compounds of its own. It turns out the answer depends heavily on how you evaluate it. We assembled 41,000 whole-cell Mycobacterium tuberculosis H37Rv measurements from ChEMBL and PubChem and trained gradient boosting and graph neural network models to predict MIC below 10 micromolar. Under random splits, both approaches looked excellent, with AUROC around 0.91. Under scaffold splits that mimic what a team really faces when moving to a new series, performance dropped to 0.74 for the boosted trees and 0.71 for the graph network.

We then tested the models prospectively on an in-house hit-to-lead program built around an indazole sulfonamide series. Of 96 newly synthesized analogues, the model ranked the top quartile with a hit rate of 41 percent, compared with 17 percent in the remainder. That is useful, but not magic. Where the model failed was informative: it consistently overrated compounds with high lipophilicity, which are easy to make active in a whole-cell assay but tend to carry poor solubility and high plasma protein binding. Adding a simple penalty for clogP above 4.5 recovered some of the lost precision and, in our hands, steered synthesis toward compounds that held up better in mouse pharmacokinetics.

The practical lesson is modest. Public data give a reasonable prior for generic antimycobacterial activity, but the ranking within a single chemical series still depends on measurements from that series. We recommend fine-tuning with as few as 40 local data points, which raised scaffold-split AUROC to 0.83 in a retrospective test. Code, trained models and the curated dataset are available under open licenses, and we describe the curation steps in enough detail for others to repeat them on their own targets.

Antimicrobial resistance is a growing threat to public health in sub-Saharan Africa, where surveillance capacity is limited and data on the local burden of resistant pathogens remain scarce. In this study, we describe the establishment and evaluation of a regional laboratory network for antimicrobial resistance surveillance in four countries: Ghana, Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania. Between January 2021 and December 2023, twelve participating hospital laboratories collected 9,862 clinical isolates, including Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus and Acinetobacter baumannii, and tested them for susceptibility following EUCAST standards.

The results show a high prevalence of resistance to third-generation cephalosporins among Enterobacterales, with 64 percent of E. coli and 81 percent of K. pneumoniae isolates producing extended-spectrum beta-lactamases. Methicillin resistance was found in 28 percent of S. aureus isolates, while carbapenem resistance in A. baumannii reached 57 percent in intensive care units. Whole-genome sequencing of a subset of 410 isolates identified CTX-M-15 as the dominant resistance determinant, and revealed several clonal lineages, such as ST131 and ST307, circulating across more than one country. Importantly, resistance patterns differed substantially between tertiary hospitals and district facilities, which suggests that national averages may hide relevant local differences.

Beyond the epidemiological findings, we evaluated the capacity-building component of the network. Laboratory staff completed a structured training programme in microbiology quality management and bioinformatics, and the proportion of laboratories passing external quality assessment increased from 42 to 83 percent over the study period. We also introduced an open-source analysis pipeline that allows local teams to process sequencing data without dependence on external partners. These findings demonstrate that investment in training and shared infrastructure can improve the quality and the local ownership of surveillance data, and they provide a basis for evidence-based antibiotic policy in the region.

Visceral leishmaniasis is a neglected tropical disease that causes an estimated 50,000 to 90,000 new cases each year, and current treatments are limited by toxicity, cost, and the need for parenteral administration. Here, we present a machine learning framework for the prediction of antileishmanial activity and its application to the virtual screening of a 2.3 million compound library. We curated a dataset of 14,860 compounds with reported activity against Leishmania donovani intracellular amastigotes from ChEMBL and the Drugs for Neglected Diseases initiative open datasets. Using extended-connectivity fingerprints and a set of physicochemical descriptors, we trained random forest, support vector machine, and directed message-passing neural network models, and evaluated them using five-fold cross-validation with scaffold-based splitting.

The best-performing model, an ensemble of the random forest and message-passing network, achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.87 and a precision-recall AUC of 0.62 on the held-out test set. Applying the ensemble to the virtual library, we selected 420 top-ranked compounds, filtered them for drug-likeness and synthetic accessibility, and purchased 96 for experimental testing. Of these, 19 compounds exhibited an EC50 below 10 micromolar against intracellular amastigotes, corresponding to a hit rate of 20 percent, which is approximately tenfold higher than the hit rate observed in conventional high-throughput screening campaigns. Seven compounds showed a selectivity index above 20 against THP-1 macrophages.

Analysis of the confirmed hits revealed enrichment in three chemotypes, including a series of 3-nitroimidazopyridines and a novel class of aminopyrazole carboxamides. Matched molecular pair analysis suggested preliminary structure-activity relationships that can guide subsequent optimization. These results demonstrate that data-driven approaches can substantially accelerate hit identification for neglected tropical diseases, and we make the trained models and the curated dataset freely available to the community to support further research.

Most generative chemistry papers report validity, uniqueness and novelty, and then stop. Those numbers are easy to get right and tell you very little about whether the molecules are worth making. We took a different angle and asked how often a generative model proposes compounds that a medicinal chemist would actually accept. We trained a SMILES-based transformer on 1.6 million ChEMBL structures, fine-tuned it with reinforcement learning toward predicted activity against Trypanosoma cruzi, and generated 50,000 candidates. Standard metrics were unremarkable: 98.7 percent valid, 91 percent unique, and a mean Tanimoto similarity to the nearest training compound of 0.42.

We then asked five experienced chemists, working independently, to review a random sample of 300 molecules and mark each as acceptable, doubtful or rejected. Only 23 percent were judged acceptable by a majority. Rejections clustered around unstable ring systems, reactive Michael acceptors, and structures that looked like they would take a dozen steps to make. Agreement among raters was only moderate (Fleiss kappa 0.41), which is itself worth knowing: what counts as a reasonable molecule depends on who you ask. A synthesizability filter based on retrosynthesis search raised acceptance to 46 percent, and adding explicit penalties for a short list of problematic substructures brought it to 58 percent.

We synthesized twelve of the accepted molecules. Three showed activity against intracellular amastigotes below 5 micromolar, one of which belongs to a scaffold absent from known Chagas disease chemotypes in our reference set. We do not claim that the model has discovered a drug. We claim that human review should be part of any benchmark for generative design, and we release the annotations so that automated filters can be trained against them. Reviewers can reuse the protocol with their own targets, and we think the extra effort is small compared with the cost of synthesizing molecules nobody wanted.

Schistosomiasis affects more than 200 million people worldwide, and treatment relies almost entirely on a single drug, praziquantel, which is poorly active against juvenile worms and for which reduced susceptibility has been reported. In this work, we investigate the repurposing of approved kinase inhibitors as antischistosomal agents using a combined computational and experimental approach. We first compiled a library of 312 clinically approved or late-stage kinase inhibitors and used homology models of Schistosoma mansoni kinases, together with similarity to known ligands, to prioritise 58 candidates for testing.

The selected compounds were evaluated in vitro against adult worms and newly transformed schistosomula at a concentration of 10 micromolar. Twenty-two compounds reduced worm motility or viability by more than 50 percent after 72 hours, and eight of them showed an IC50 below 5 micromolar. Among them, a pan-tyrosine kinase inhibitor and a Polo-like kinase inhibitor were the most potent, with IC50 values of 0.9 and 1.4 micromolar against adult worms, respectively. Importantly, both compounds were also active against juvenile worms, which is a clear advantage compared with praziquantel. Cytotoxicity against HEK293 cells was limited, with selectivity indexes between 6 and 15.

In a murine model of chronic infection, oral treatment with the Polo-like kinase inhibitor at 50 mg/kg for five days reduced the total worm burden by 63 percent and the egg load in the liver by 71 percent. Although the efficacy was lower than the one observed with praziquantel, combination of both drugs gave an additive effect and reduced worm burden by 88 percent. Our results suggest that kinase inhibitors represent a valuable source of starting points for antischistosomal drug discovery, and that the use of computational prioritisation can reduce the experimental cost of repurposing campaigns.

The rapid and accurate prediction of absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion and toxicity properties is critical for reducing attrition in drug discovery. However, the reliability of machine learning models for ADMET endpoints is often limited by data heterogeneity, small dataset sizes, and uncertainty about the applicability domain. In this study, we present a systematic evaluation of multitask and single-task approaches for the prediction of 22 ADMET endpoints using a curated collection of 380,000 measurements drawn from public sources, including ChEMBL, the Therapeutics Data Commons and published literature.

We compared five molecular representations, including Morgan fingerprints, RDKit descriptors, and pretrained embeddings from two chemical language models, in combination with random forests, LightGBM, and Chemprop. Models were evaluated using scaffold-based and temporal splits, and uncertainty was quantified using conformal prediction. Our results show that multitask Chemprop models with pretrained embeddings achieved the best average performance, with a mean R-squared of 0.61 for regression tasks and a mean AUROC of 0.83 for classification tasks. However, simple fingerprint-based LightGBM models remained competitive for endpoints with abundant data, such as lipophilicity and microsomal stability, and outperformed deep models on 7 of the 22 endpoints.

Conformal prediction provided well-calibrated confidence intervals, with empirical coverage within two percentage points of the nominal level of 90 percent across all tasks. Importantly, prediction intervals were substantially wider for compounds outside the training distribution, which allowed us to flag 14 percent of an external test set as unreliable. External validation on 1,200 compounds from an independent pharmaceutical dataset confirmed that performance decreased by 8 to 15 percent relative to internal testing, highlighting the importance of realistic evaluation. We provide all models as open-source packages with standardized interfaces, facilitating their integration into existing drug discovery workflows and enabling researchers in resource-limited settings to access state-of-the-art property prediction.

Getting a cheminformatics tool adopted outside the group that wrote it is harder than writing it. This is the story of ten years with a small open-source Python library for standardizing, deduplicating and featurizing molecular datasets, and what we changed after we looked honestly at who was using it and who had given up. The library started as a collection of scripts we used internally for antimalarial QSAR work. It now has about 1,900 stars on GitHub and roughly 28,000 monthly downloads, though download counts are a poor guide to actual use.

To find out more, we surveyed 214 users and interviewed 17, including researchers in Nigeria, Uganda, Brazil and India. Three obstacles came up repeatedly. First, installation failed on older machines and on institutional networks with restricted access; a fix as plain as providing an offline wheel bundle removed the single most common complaint. Second, documentation assumed a knowledge of RDKit conventions that students did not have. Third, people did not trust results they could not trace, and wanted to see exactly what each standardization step had changed. We responded with a lightweight audit log that records every structure modification, a set of tutorials written with and for students at two African universities, and a test suite that runs on a laptop in under four minutes.

Since these changes, median time to a first successful run, measured by anonymous opt-in telemetry, fell from 47 to 11 minutes, and the proportion of issues from users outside Europe and North America rose from 9 to 31 percent. The library is not glamorous, and what it does is mundane. But mundane tools are what most of our field actually depends on, and we think software papers should say more about maintenance, onboarding and failure.

Repurposing of approved drugs is an attractive strategy for the rapid identification of antiviral therapies, especially for emerging viruses for which no specific treatment exists. In this study, we describe a high-content imaging screen of 2,150 approved and investigational drugs against Chikungunya virus in Vero E6 and human skin fibroblast cells. Compounds were tested at a single concentration of 10 micromolar, and antiviral activity was measured by immunofluorescence detection of viral E2 protein, together with a nuclear stain to assess cell viability.

The primary screen identified 74 compounds that reduced infection by more than 70 percent without significant cytotoxicity. After dose-response confirmation, 29 compounds showed an EC50 below 5 micromolar in both cell lines. The confirmed hits were enriched in several pharmacological classes, including cationic amphiphilic drugs, nucleoside analogues, and inhibitors of host pyrimidine biosynthesis. Time-of-addition experiments indicated that the cationic amphiphilic compounds acted mainly at the entry stage, whereas the nucleoside analogues and the dihydroorotate dehydrogenase inhibitors were active also when added four hours after infection, consistent with an effect on viral replication. Combination of the DHODH inhibitor brequinar with the nucleoside analogue favipiravir produced a synergistic effect, with a combination index of 0.42, and reduced viral titres by 3.1 logs.

To prioritise compounds for further studies, we integrated the screening data with predicted pharmacokinetic properties and with reported plasma concentrations in humans. Eleven compounds reached exposures in the range of their in vitro EC50 at approved doses. Our study provides a well-characterised list of repurposing candidates for Chikungunya virus and highlights host pathways that can be explored as targets for broad-spectrum antiviral strategies. All primary data are shared in an open repository to enable reuse by the community.

Tuberculosis remains the leading cause of death from a single infectious agent worldwide, with an estimated 10.6 million new cases and 1.3 million deaths reported in 2022. The standard six-month regimen for drug-susceptible disease is lengthy and burdensome, and the rise of multidrug-resistant and extensively drug-resistant strains has made treatment even more challenging. Although the approval of bedaquiline, pretomanid, and delamanid marked a significant step forward, resistance to these agents has already been reported, underscoring the continuing need for new chemical entities with novel mechanisms of action.

Hit-to-lead optimization in tuberculosis drug discovery presents unique challenges. Mycobacterium tuberculosis possesses a thick, lipid-rich cell envelope that limits the permeability of many compounds, and activity in biochemical assays frequently fails to translate into whole-cell potency. Furthermore, the pathogen can persist in a non-replicating state within granulomas, where drug penetration and bacterial physiology differ markedly from those in standard culture conditions. As a result, compounds that appear promising in vitro often show disappointing efficacy in vivo, and the attrition rate in the pipeline remains high.

In recent years, phenotypic screening has re-emerged as a productive strategy for identifying novel antitubercular scaffolds. Large-scale campaigns by academic consortia and pharmaceutical companies have yielded several promising series, including the indolcarboxamides, the imidazopyridine amides, and the 4-aminoquinolone piperidine amides. However, the progression of these hits requires careful balancing of potency, physicochemical properties, and safety. Lipophilicity, in particular, has been identified as a key driver of whole-cell activity, yet high lipophilicity is also associated with poor solubility, increased metabolic clearance, and off-target toxicity. Optimizing ligand efficiency and lipophilic ligand efficiency during the hit-to-lead phase is therefore essential.

Computational approaches offer a means of navigating these trade-offs more efficiently. Machine learning models trained on whole-cell data can prioritize compounds for synthesis, while physics-based methods can provide insight into binding modes and guide structure-based design when target information is available. In this work, we integrate these approaches in the optimization of a novel series of pyrazolopyrimidines active against M. tuberculosis. By combining matched molecular pair analysis, predictive modeling, and iterative experimental validation, we aim to demonstrate a streamlined workflow that can accelerate progression from initial hit to a lead with in vivo proof of concept.

It is tempting to read the recent run of successes in machine learning for molecules as proof that the hard problems are solved. They are not. Anyone who has tried to use a published ADMET model on a real project knows the experience: the paper reports a respectable correlation, you run your own compounds through it, and the predictions land nowhere near your measurements. Part of this is the usual story about distribution shift. A larger part, we think, is that the field has been rather casual about what a prediction is for.

Consider microsomal stability. Public datasets mix human, rat and mouse measurements, different incubation conditions, different units, and values that were truncated at assay limits and then quietly recorded as exact numbers. A model trained on this soup learns to reproduce the soup. When a chemist asks whether a new analogue will be cleared quickly, what she wants is a ranking within her own series, with some honest sense of how far to trust it. A global model with an R-squared of 0.6 on random splits can be close to useless at that task, because most of the variance it explains lies between series rather than within them.

None of this means the models are worthless. In our experience they are useful in two narrow situations: triage of very large virtual libraries, where a modest enrichment saves real money, and flagging of obvious liabilities, such as extreme lipophilicity or known toxicophores, that a team would rather learn about before synthesis. They are much less useful for fine discrimination between close analogues, and we should stop evaluating them as though they were.

The studies we describe below were designed with that distinction in mind. We report performance within chemical series as well as across them, we keep assay conditions as covariates rather than discarding them, and we state in advance how large an improvement over a trivial baseline would change a synthesis decision. That last requirement turned out to be the most difficult to meet, and the most instructive.

Capacity building in drug discovery is increasingly recognised as a prerequisite for the development of treatments that respond to the needs of populations in low- and middle-income countries. Africa carries a disproportionate share of the global burden of infectious diseases such as malaria, tuberculosis and neglected tropical diseases, yet the continent contributes less than two percent of global research output in pharmaceutical sciences. This imbalance has consequences not only for scientific equity but also for the relevance of the research agenda, since priorities are often defined by institutions that are geographically and culturally distant from the affected communities.

Several initiatives have attempted to address this gap. Programmes such as the Drug Discovery and Development Centre at the University of Cape Town (H3D) have demonstrated that world-class medicinal chemistry and pharmacology can be established on the continent, and have delivered clinical candidates for malaria and tuberculosis. Nevertheless, such centres remain few, and most African researchers still work without access to the computational infrastructure, curated datasets and training opportunities that are taken for granted elsewhere. Language barriers, unreliable internet connectivity and limited access to commercial software further restrict participation.

Computational methods offer a particular opportunity in this context. Compared with wet-laboratory research, computational drug discovery requires relatively modest investment in equipment, and open-source tools allow researchers to work without licensing costs. However, the availability of software alone is not sufficient. Sustainable capacity requires that local scientists are trained not only to use existing tools but also to adapt, maintain and develop them, and that they are integrated into international networks as full partners rather than as data providers.

In this article, we describe a training programme in cheminformatics and machine learning that was delivered to 85 early-career researchers from 14 African countries between 2020 and 2023. We discuss the design of the curriculum, the use of mentoring and project-based learning, and the outcomes observed in terms of publications, open-source contributions and career progression. We also reflect on the difficulties encountered, including the unequal access to computing resources, and we propose recommendations for the design of future programmes with a long-term perspective.

The discovery of new antimalarial drugs has historically relied on natural products and on the modification of existing scaffolds, such as the quinolines and the artemisinins. However, the spread of parasite resistance has repeatedly eroded the clinical value of these drug classes. Resistance to chloroquine emerged in the late 1950s and spread across most malaria-endemic regions, and partial resistance to artemisinin, characterized by delayed parasite clearance and associated with mutations in the Kelch13 propeller domain, has now been confirmed in Southeast Asia and, more recently, in Rwanda, Uganda, and Eritrea. These developments raise the prospect that artemisinin-based combination therapies may lose efficacy in the region that bears over 90 percent of the global malaria burden.

The target product profiles defined by the Medicines for Malaria Venture emphasize several key attributes for next-generation antimalarials: activity against resistant parasites, a mechanism of action distinct from existing drugs, potential for single-dose cure, and activity against multiple parasite life-cycle stages, including the liver stage and the transmissible gametocyte stage. Meeting all these criteria simultaneously is a considerable challenge, and few compounds have progressed through clinical development. Ganaplacide, cipargamin, and ZY-19489 represent recent advances, but the pipeline remains thin and attrition is expected.

Open-source and open-access models of drug discovery have played an increasingly important role in addressing this challenge. The release of the Malaria Box, the Pathogen Box, and the GSK Tres Cantos antimalarial set provided the community with thousands of validated starting points and associated bioactivity data. These resources have enabled numerous academic groups to initiate drug discovery programs, and they have supplied the training data for machine learning models of antiplasmodial activity. Notably, models trained on these datasets have been used to prioritize compounds from large virtual libraries, resulting in hit rates that substantially exceed those from random screening.

Despite this progress, important gaps remain. Many published models are not accompanied by usable code, standardized benchmarks are lacking, and little attention has been paid to the applicability of models to chemical space beyond that of the original datasets. In the present study, we address these limitations by developing and rigorously evaluating a suite of open-source predictive models for antiplasmodial activity.

Our results sit uneasily with part of the literature, and it is worth saying why. Several groups have reported that deep neural networks trained on public antiplasmodial data outperform fingerprint-based random forests by wide margins. We did not see this. Across three splitting strategies and five random seeds, the best deep model was within 0.02 AUROC of a random forest on Morgan fingerprints, and the difference vanished entirely once we tuned the forest properly. We went looking for an error in our pipeline for some weeks, and found a couple of minor ones, but none that changed the picture.

What did we do differently? Mostly, we were stricter about leakage. The Tres Cantos and Malaria Box sets contain many near-duplicate compounds, often the same scaffold with a different salt form or a one-carbon extension. Splitting at the level of individual molecules therefore puts siblings on both sides of the split, and any model that memorizes local structure will score well. When we clustered the data at a Tanimoto threshold of 0.6 and kept whole clusters together, the apparent advantage of the large models shrank. We cannot rule out that they would still win with more data, or with better pretraining, but on the datasets that antimalarial chemists actually have, the gap is small.

There is a more general point here. A benchmark is a claim about the world, and a leaky benchmark makes a false claim with great confidence. Several of the high numbers in the literature were probably obtained without malice, using standard splitting utilities that behave reasonably on other kinds of data. It is also worth noting that our own earlier work was not immune: a reanalysis of our 2019 models with cluster-based splits lowered their reported AUROC from 0.89 to 0.78.

The practical consequence is that choosing between model families should matter less to a project team than choosing a validation scheme that resembles their deployment. We return to this in the next section, where we describe a simple protocol that teams can apply to their own data.

Chagas disease, caused by the protozoan parasite Trypanosoma cruzi, affects approximately six to seven million people, mainly in Latin America, and is increasingly detected in non-endemic countries due to migration. The current treatment relies on two nitroheterocyclic drugs, benznidazole and nifurtimox, which were developed more than fifty years ago. Both drugs are associated with frequent adverse effects that lead to treatment discontinuation in up to 30 percent of patients, and their efficacy in the chronic phase of the disease is variable. Therefore, the development of safer and more effective therapies remains an unmet medical need.

The drug discovery pipeline for Chagas disease has been disappointing in recent years. Azole inhibitors of the sterol 14-alpha-demethylase, such as posaconazole and fosravuconazole, showed excellent activity in preclinical models but failed in clinical trials, with a high rate of relapse compared with benznidazole. These results raised important questions about the predictive value of the available in vitro and in vivo models, and about the role of the parasite dormancy in treatment failure. It is now suggested that a fraction of intracellular amastigotes may enter a non-replicating state that is less susceptible to many compounds, which could explain why drugs that are potent in standard assays may fail to achieve sterile cure.

To address these challenges, new screening strategies have been proposed. High-content imaging assays that measure the effect of compounds on intracellular amastigotes in different host cell types, together with washout experiments that quantify parasite recrudescence, may provide a more stringent filter in the early phases of drug discovery. In addition, the proteasome inhibitor GNF6702 and the oxaborole AN15368 have shown curative activity in animal models, supporting the idea that new mechanisms of action may overcome the limitations of previous approaches.

In this context, computational methods can contribute by integrating the growing amount of public data and by identifying chemical series with a higher probability of success. In the present work, we use a machine learning approach to predict compounds with fast-kill kinetics and low recrudescence, and we validate our predictions experimentally using a panel of 64 compounds from the Chagas Box.

Antimicrobial resistance is widely recognized as one of the greatest threats to global health in the twenty-first century. A recent analysis estimated that bacterial antimicrobial resistance was directly responsible for 1.27 million deaths in 2019 and contributed to nearly five million more, with the highest burden in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia. Gram-negative pathogens, particularly carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Enterobacterales, are of critical concern, as therapeutic options for these organisms are severely limited.

The antibiotic pipeline has not kept pace with the evolution of resistance. Between 2017 and 2023, only a small number of new antibacterial agents were approved, and most of them were derivatives of existing classes. Discovery of truly novel antibiotics is hampered by the difficulty of achieving sufficient accumulation in Gram-negative bacteria, whose outer membrane and efflux pumps act in concert to exclude most small molecules. Predictive rules for compound penetration, such as the eNTRy rules, have provided useful guidance, but they were derived from a limited number of compounds and do not capture all the complexity of the process.

Machine learning has recently emerged as a powerful tool to address these challenges. Landmark studies have shown that graph neural networks trained on growth inhibition data can identify structurally novel antibiotics, including halicin and abaucin, from large chemical libraries. Furthermore, explainable approaches have enabled the identification of substructures associated with activity and low cytotoxicity, leading to the discovery of new structural classes active against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. These successes highlight the potential of data-driven approaches to explore chemical space beyond traditional medicinal chemistry paradigms.

However, several limitations remain. Training data are typically generated in a small number of laboratories using a limited set of strains, and may not reflect the diversity of clinical isolates, particularly those from low- and middle-income countries. In addition, models are rarely evaluated for their ability to predict activity against resistant strains, and the choice of negative examples can greatly affect performance. In this study, we address these issues by constructing a multi-strain dataset of 22,000 compounds and evaluating predictive models under conditions that reflect real-world discovery scenarios.

Open-source cheminformatics owes a great deal to a small number of people who kept a handful of packages alive on evenings and weekends. RDKit, Open Babel and a few others became load-bearing infrastructure for thousands of laboratories without anyone ever deciding that they should. This is a fragile arrangement, and it is only now getting the attention it deserves.

What the next generation of tools should look like is a different question, and one on which we hold a particular view. The field has spent a decade building models, and surprisingly little effort on making them usable by someone who did not build them. We have lost count of the published predictors whose repository contains a notebook that ran once, in 2021, on a machine nobody can name. Dependencies drift, checkpoints go missing, and a model that cost six months of graduate work becomes unrunnable within a couple of years. For a chemist in a small laboratory, without a software engineer down the corridor, such a tool might as well not exist.

The alternative is not complicated, though it is unglamorous. A model should come with its environment, a fixed input and output format, a small test that confirms it still gives the same answer, and metadata saying what it was trained on and what it should not be used for. If a hundred models share those conventions, a researcher can run any of them with the same command, compare several on the same compounds, and replace one with another when something better arrives. That is the idea behind several recent efforts to build shared model repositories, including the one we describe here.

We should be candid about the costs. Standardization removes flexibility, and some interesting models do not fit neatly into tabular inputs and outputs. Maintenance is also unending: every model in a hub is a promise to keep it working. Our experience suggests the burden is manageable if most of the checking is automated, and if the community sees itself as a collective responsible for the repository rather than a set of users of it.

Generative models for molecular design have attracted considerable attention in recent years, as they promise to accelerate the exploration of the vast chemical space, which is estimated to contain more than 10^60 drug-like molecules. Different architectures have been proposed, including recurrent neural networks, variational autoencoders, generative adversarial networks, and more recently transformers and diffusion models. These methods can be trained to reproduce the distribution of known bioactive molecules and, when combined with reinforcement learning or Bayesian optimisation, to generate compounds optimised toward multiple objectives.

Despite the enthusiasm, the evaluation of generative models remains problematic. Metrics commonly reported in the literature, such as validity, uniqueness and novelty, are easy to satisfy and do not guarantee that the generated molecules are synthesisable or have the desired biological activity. Moreover, many reported success stories rely on in silico scoring functions, which are themselves approximate and can be exploited by the generator in unexpected ways. In consequence, the number of studies that report the experimental validation of generated molecules is still limited, and the hit rates are difficult to compare across different targets and assay formats.

In the case of neglected diseases, additional constraints apply. The amount of available training data is small, and the molecules should be cheap to synthesise, since the final product has to be affordable in low-resource settings. Therefore, the generative process should incorporate considerations of cost and synthetic accessibility from the beginning, rather than as a post-hoc filter. This requires the integration of retrosynthesis tools and of building-block availability, which is not trivial for laboratories in countries where chemical suppliers are limited and import times are long.

In this work, we propose a generative framework in which candidate molecules are restricted to those that can be prepared in at most four steps from a list of 3,500 commercially available building blocks. We apply this framework to the design of inhibitors of Schistosoma mansoni thioredoxin glutathione reductase, and we show that the constrained approach produces molecules with comparable predicted activity to the unconstrained model, but with a significantly lower estimated synthetic cost.

I read this submission with interest and some frustration. The authors have assembled a useful dataset of 6,200 compounds tested against Mycobacterium tuberculosis in macrophage infection assays, and they show that a random forest model trained on it can pick out the more potent chemotypes. The paper is short, readable and mostly honest. It also overreaches in the discussion, which I will come to.

The strongest part is the data. Intracellular activity is much scarcer in the public domain than axenic MIC, and anyone working on hit-to-lead will want this. The authors also deserve credit for describing how they handled compounds measured in several laboratories, and for keeping the replicate values rather than averaging them away.

My main concern is the claim in the abstract that the model "enables rational prioritization of novel scaffolds." The evidence does not go that far. All reported performance comes from fivefold cross-validation on randomly assigned compounds. Looking at the supplementary table, I count 14 scaffolds that each contribute more than 100 compounds, so a random split lets the model learn the series and then recognize its siblings. What I would like to see is leave-one-series-out validation. If performance holds up, the claim stands; if it collapses, the authors have still produced a useful dataset, and they should say so.

Second, the label. Activity is defined as at least a 1 log reduction in bacterial load at 10 micromolar, but the dataset spans assays with different readouts, durations and cell types. I do not know how much of the model's signal reflects chemistry and how much reflects which laboratory generated the data. A simple check would be to predict the source laboratory from the fingerprints and see how well that works.

Third, the lack of any comparison to a lipophilicity-only baseline. In whole-cell tuberculosis data, clogP alone is a surprisingly strong predictor, and I suspect the forest is partly rediscovering it.

Minor: the SHAP figure is attractive but uninterpretable at the scale shown; the Methods give hyperparameters but not the search ranges; two references appear to be duplicated; and the code repository lacks a license.

I recommend major revision. The work could be a solid contribution with a more cautious framing and a stricter evaluation.

The manuscript under review presents an open-source Python package for the standardisation and curation of chemical datasets, intended to facilitate the construction of machine learning models for ADMET prediction. The authors demonstrate the tool on ten public datasets and show that the curation procedure improves the performance of random forest models by an average of 4 percent in R-squared. The topic is of clear interest, since data quality is a recognised bottleneck of the field, and the release of the software under a permissive licence is appreciated.

Among the strengths of the work, I would highlight the modular design of the package, the comprehensive documentation, and the inclusion of unit tests covering 87 percent of the code. The authors have also taken care to make the pipeline reproducible, with fixed versions of dependencies and a container image.

Nevertheless, I have some concerns that should be addressed before publication. The most important one relates to the evidence for the claimed benefit. The improvement of 4 percent is reported without any measure of variability, and with ten datasets and a single random split it is not possible to know whether the difference is statistically meaningful. I recommend repeating the experiments with at least ten different seeds and reporting means with standard deviations or confidence intervals, together with a paired statistical test.

Furthermore, it is not clear which components of the pipeline are responsible for the improvement. The workflow includes salt stripping, tautomer canonicalisation, charge neutralisation, removal of duplicates, and filtering of outliers. An ablation study would help the reader to understand which steps matter, and would be useful to developers of other tools. In particular, the outlier filter, which removes values more than three standard deviations from the mean, could eliminate genuine activity cliffs, and the authors should discuss this risk.

In addition, the comparison with existing tools, such as the ChEMBL structure pipeline and MolVS, is limited to a qualitative table of features. A quantitative comparison on the same datasets would strengthen the manuscript considerably.

Regarding minor points, some figures contain text that is too small, the English requires light editing in the Discussion, and the installation instructions for Windows should be verified.

In summary, the work is useful and well engineered, but the evaluation needs to be strengthened. I recommend major revision.

Summary of the submission: The authors report a phenotypic screen of 1,920 compounds against Leishmania donovani intracellular amastigotes, identify 38 confirmed hits, and characterize a lead series of triazolopyrimidines with in vitro EC50 values between 0.3 and 2 micromolar. One compound is evaluated in a mouse model of visceral leishmaniasis and shows a 72 percent reduction in liver parasite burden at 25 mg/kg orally for five days.

Strengths: The work addresses an important neglected disease and the screening data are of good quality, with a Z-prime above 0.7 across plates and appropriate use of miltefosine and amphotericin B as reference compounds. The structure-activity relationship table is informative, and the authors have included the cytotoxicity data for all analogues. The in vivo experiment, while limited, is a valuable addition.

Major concerns: First, the mechanism of action is not addressed. The Discussion suggests that the compounds target a parasite kinase, but no evidence is provided beyond the structural similarity to known kinase inhibitors. Without target engagement data, such as a thermal shift assay, resistant mutant analysis, or biochemical inhibition, this statement should be removed or clearly marked as speculation.

Second, the in vivo study uses a single dose level and groups of five animals, and no pharmacokinetic data are presented. It is therefore impossible to determine whether the efficacy results from adequate exposure, or whether the lack of dose response reflects a plateau. I would recommend including plasma exposure data, a dose-response experiment, and a statistical analysis of the efficacy findings.

Third, the claim that the series has favorable drug-like properties is not fully supported. The kinetic solubility of the lead compound is 3 micromolar at pH 7.4, which is low, and the microsomal half-life in mouse is 9 minutes. These data are shown in the supplementary information but not discussed in the main text.

Fourth, the cytotoxicity counter-screen was performed with HepG2 cells, which is not the most relevant host cell. THP-1 or primary macrophages, which are used in the efficacy assay, should be used.

Minor points: The title overstates the findings. Several compound identifiers in Table 1 do not match those in the supplementary file. The statistical tests used in Figure 5 are not specified. The ethics statement for the animal work should include the approval number.

Recommendation: major revision.

This paper claims that a transformer pretrained on 800 million molecules, then fine-tuned on a few thousand schistosomiasis assay results, beats everything else by a large margin. If true, it would matter. I am not convinced it is true, and I will try to explain why without being unkind, because the work has real merit.

What I liked: the authors provide fine-tuning data that were collected under consistent conditions at a single institute, which is rare. They compare against six baselines instead of the usual two. The writing is good, and I appreciated that the limitations paragraph was written by someone who clearly thought about the problem.

What worries me begins with the test set. It contains 310 compounds, of which 22 are active. With so few positives, an AUROC of 0.91 has a confidence interval wide enough to include the best baseline. The authors report a single number from a single run, and the improvement over the random forest is 0.03. I would like to see bootstrapped intervals and repeated splits. I suspect that the headline claim will not survive this treatment, and I would rather the authors found out than a reader.

The hyperparameter search also looks unequal. The pretrained model got a sweep over learning rate, layers frozen and dropout, which seems a lot of effort, while the random forest appears to have been run with defaults. This is a common problem and I do not suggest bad faith, but it makes the comparison unfair.

A further point: the pretraining set almost certainly includes many of the test compounds, since it was drawn from public databases that overlap with the source of the schistosomiasis data. The authors should check for this directly and remove any overlap.

Finally, I would have liked a short discussion of cost. A model that requires a GPU cluster to fine-tune is not obviously useful to a laboratory in Kampala or Khartoum, and the authors work in precisely this field.

Minor points: please define active in the figure legends, fix the inconsistent y-axis in Figure 3, and cite the original scaffold-split paper.

I would be glad to see a revised version. Major revision.

This study reports the repurposing screening of 1,600 approved drugs against SARS-CoV-2 in Calu-3 cells, followed by the evaluation of 21 hits in a hamster infection model. The authors identify three compounds, an antihistamine, an antifungal and an antipsychotic, that reduce viral RNA in the lungs by more than one log at the tested doses. The paper is clearly organised and the topic remains relevant for pandemic preparedness.

I appreciate several aspects of the work. The screening protocol is well described, the authors used two independent readouts (viral RNA and cytopathic effect), and they included remdesivir as a positive control in each plate. In addition, the choice of Calu-3 cells, which express TMPRSS2, is more physiologically relevant than the Vero cells used in many previous screens.

However, there are important issues that limit the strength of the conclusions. First, the concentrations needed for activity in vitro are in the range of 5 to 15 micromolar, whereas the reported human plasma concentrations at approved doses for these drugs are below 1 micromolar for the antihistamine and the antipsychotic. The authors do not discuss this gap, but it is critical for the claim of repurposing potential. In the hamster experiment, the doses used (50 to 100 mg/kg) are several times higher than the human equivalent dose, and plasma levels were not measured.

Second, the three active compounds are cationic amphiphilic drugs, a class that is known to produce antiviral effects in cell culture through phospholipidosis and lysosomal alkalinisation, and that has often failed in clinical studies. The authors should test whether the activity is lost in cells lacking the relevant endosomal route or when phospholipidosis is excluded, and they should discuss earlier negative clinical results.

Third, the hamster study has small groups (n = 4) and the statistical analysis is not clear. Please indicate the test used and whether multiple comparisons were corrected.

Regarding minor points, the figure legends are incomplete, the units in Table 2 are inconsistent, and several recent studies on the same compounds are not cited.

Overall, the screening data have value, but the repurposing conclusion is not yet supported by the evidence. I suggest major revision.

This manuscript presents a capacity-building programme in bioinformatics and computational drug discovery delivered across five African universities and evaluates its outcomes over three years. The authors report that 142 trainees completed the programme, that 64 percent subsequently contributed to a peer-reviewed publication or open-source project, and that participating institutions established two new computational research groups.

The manuscript has several strengths. The programme is well described, the partnership model is thoughtful, and the emphasis on local ownership and open resources is aligned with current thinking on research equity. The paper also includes honest discussion of the challenges encountered, such as unreliable connectivity and staff turnover.

My main concern is the evaluation design. Outcomes are assessed through a post-programme survey with a response rate of 58 percent, and no comparison group is used. As such, it is difficult to attribute the reported outcomes to the programme itself, as opposed to the selection of motivated participants. The authors should discuss selection bias explicitly, report the characteristics of non-respondents where possible, and ideally compare outcomes to a group of applicants who were not admitted.

In addition, the metric of contribution to a publication or open-source project is broad. Authorship position, the nature of the contribution, and the time to first output should be reported, as these would allow readers to judge the depth of the impact. Likewise, the claim that the programme established two new research groups requires evidence, such as funding obtained or personnel hired.

The paper would also benefit from a cost analysis. Readers planning similar programmes will want to know the cost per trainee and the sustainability of the model once initial funding ends.

Another point relates to authorship. Most authors are affiliated with institutions in Europe and North America, and the manuscript would be strengthened by a clearer account of how African partners shaped the design and the analysis.

Minor comments include the need for a flow diagram of participants, correction of several typographical errors, and clarification of how the trainees' countries were represented. I recommend minor to moderate revision.

The authors present a tool for predicting hERG inhibition and claim it is "state of the art". I think the tool is probably decent, but the manuscript does not demonstrate it.

Briefly, the model is a multitask message-passing network trained on 14,000 compounds with hERG measurements, with auxiliary tasks for other ion channels. They report AUROC 0.89 on a test set and show a web server, which I tried. It worked, and returned a prediction in a few seconds, which is more than I can say for many papers I review.

My first problem is that the test set is a random 10 percent of the same data pool used for training. hERG data are heavily clustered because medicinal chemistry papers report many analogues of one series, so this is the easiest possible evaluation. The authors do mention a second test set from a pharmaceutical company, but it only appears in the supplement, and the AUROC there is 0.71. That is the real number, and it belongs in the abstract.

Second, the threshold. hERG is a continuous property, and the 10 micromolar cutoff used here is conventional but arbitrary. Most compounds near the threshold are effectively coin flips, and the model should be assessed on whether it ranks compounds, not just classifies them. A regression analysis, or at least performance stratified by distance from the threshold, would be informative.

Third, no uncertainty is attached to the predictions on the web server. A user submitting a macrocycle or a PROTAC will get a confident number with no warning that such compounds are far outside the training data. Adding an applicability domain flag would take an afternoon and would make the tool safer to use.

I also have questions about the licence on the training data, because some of it appears to come from a commercial database.

Smaller things: Figure 2 shows ROC curves without confidence bands, the Methods do not state the number of epochs, and the phrase "state of the art" should be dropped unless the authors compare against recently published models, of which several exist.

Recommendation: major revision. I would like to see this published once it is properly tested.

The manuscript describes a generative model based on a variational autoencoder for the design of new antibacterial molecules, with the goal of overcoming the efflux-mediated resistance of Pseudomonas aeruginosa. The authors generate 100,000 molecules, select 30 by a combination of predicted activity and synthetic accessibility, and report that 6 of them inhibit the growth of the PAO1 strain with MIC values of 8 to 32 micrograms per mL. I find the topic important and the combination of design and experiment valuable.

Regarding strengths, the paper is well structured, the training set is described in detail, and the authors report negative results for 24 compounds, which is not common and is appreciated. The inclusion of an efflux-deficient strain to investigate the role of efflux is also a good experimental decision.

With respect to weaknesses, first, the novelty of the generated active molecules is not demonstrated. The authors state that the compounds are novel, but the only evidence is that their maximum Tanimoto similarity to the training set is below 0.5. Substructure searches in public databases, such as PubChem and ChEMBL, and a comparison with known antibacterial classes should be provided. Two of the six active compounds contain a fluoroquinolone-like core and may be simple analogues of ciprofloxacin.

Second, the reported MIC values are relatively weak, and it is not clear that they would be of interest for further development. The authors should compare them with those of reference antibiotics tested in the same experiment, and discuss whether the activity could be explained by non-specific membrane effects. A cytotoxicity assay against mammalian cells is missing.

Third, the experimental section does not mention how many biological replicates were done, and the MIC values are given without ranges. Following the CLSI guidelines, at least three independent replicates should be reported.

Fourth, the selection of 30 compounds involved manual choices that are not documented. The authors should explain how the choices were made, as this is relevant for reproducibility.

As minor points, the figure with the chemical structures is of poor resolution and the text contains several grammatical errors, particularly in the Introduction.

In summary, I consider the study interesting but incomplete. My recommendation is major revision.

This paper introduces a benchmark for evaluating machine learning models on neglected tropical disease bioactivity data, comprising 12 datasets covering leishmaniasis, Chagas disease, human African trypanosomiasis, and schistosomiasis, together with baseline results for eight model types. The authors argue that existing benchmarks are dominated by oncology and central nervous system targets and do not reflect the data scarcity characteristic of neglected diseases.

I believe the proposal is timely and the benchmark could become a useful resource. The datasets are carefully curated, the provenance of each is documented, and the authors have provided a standard evaluation protocol with predefined splits. The inclusion of low-data regimes, with training sets as small as 150 compounds, is a particularly welcome feature.

There are, however, several points that require attention. First, the datasets differ greatly in size and class balance, ranging from 210 to 9,800 compounds and from 2 to 41 percent actives, yet the headline metric is the mean AUROC across datasets. This metric hides differences in difficulty and gives equal weight to datasets of very different reliability. I suggest reporting precision-recall metrics and enrichment at the top 1 percent, which better reflect the use case of virtual screening, and presenting results per dataset with confidence intervals.

Second, the predefined splits are scaffold-based, but no temporal splits are provided. For a benchmark that aims to reflect prospective use, temporal splits where available should be included.

Third, the label noise in these datasets is not addressed. Many measurements come from single-concentration screens with high false-positive rates, and some actives may not be confirmed by dose-response. The authors should quantify the proportion of confirmed actives in each dataset.

Fourth, the benchmark may suffer from overlap between datasets, as many compounds are tested against multiple parasites. Please report the extent of this overlap and clarify how it was handled in the splits.

Fifth, the licensing terms of each source should be listed, since this affects reuse.

Minor points include inconsistent naming of datasets between the text and the tables, a missing description of the hyperparameter optimisation, and the need for a public leaderboard.

I recommend minor revision.

Specific Aim 1: Develop and validate machine learning models for the prediction of antiplasmodial activity against multidrug-resistant Plasmodium falciparum. We will assemble a curated dataset of more than 40,000 compounds with measured activity against drug-sensitive and drug-resistant parasite strains, drawing on ChEMBL, PubChem, the Malaria Box, and unpublished screening data from our collaborators at the University of Cape Town and the Kenya Medical Research Institute. We will train and compare graph neural networks, gradient boosting, and pretrained chemical language models using scaffold-based and temporal validation to reflect real-world use. The expected outcome is a set of open-source models with quantified uncertainty and defined applicability domains, achieving a minimum AUROC of 0.80 on external validation compounds.

Specific Aim 2: Experimentally validate model predictions through prospective screening. Using the models from Aim 1, we will rank a virtual library of 1.5 million commercially available compounds and select 400 for purchase and testing against the 3D7 and Dd2 strains, as well as against a panel of recent Ugandan clinical isolates. Compounds with an EC50 below 1 micromolar and a selectivity index above 30 will advance to confirmatory dose-response testing, early ADME profiling, and gametocytocidal activity assessment. We anticipate that the prospective hit rate will exceed 10 percent, at least five times higher than that of conventional high-throughput screening.

Specific Aim 3: Strengthen computational drug discovery capacity in East Africa. We will train 30 early-career researchers at three partner institutions in Uganda, Kenya, and Tanzania through a combination of intensive workshops, remote mentoring, and a paid six-month research placement. Training will cover cheminformatics, machine learning, and responsible data management, and all materials will be released under open licenses. Success will be measured by the number of trainees who complete independent projects, contribute to open-source repositories, and obtain follow-on funding.

Significance: The emergence of artemisinin partial resistance in Africa represents a critical threat to malaria control. By combining predictive modeling, experimental validation, and local capacity building, this project will generate new antimalarial starting points and, equally importantly, will create a sustainable community of African scientists able to lead drug discovery for diseases that affect their populations. All models, datasets, and protocols will be made openly available, in line with the principles of open science and equitable partnership.

The case for this project starts with a plain observation: we keep making tuberculosis compounds that are potent and then stop at the same wall. Whole-cell activity is easy to get when lipophilicity goes up. Solubility, clearance and plasma protein binding then go the wrong way, and the series dies in mouse pharmacokinetics eighteen months after it looked promising. Over the past six years we have seen this happen to three of our own series, including an indazole sulfonamide class that reached MIC values of 0.05 micromolar and never exposed a mouse long enough to matter.

We propose to attack that problem directly in the hit-to-lead phase. The approach has two parts. The first is a set of matched-pair models, trained on our own measurements of about 2,800 compounds, that predict how a particular chemical change shifts MIC, kinetic solubility and microsomal stability together. The aim is not an accurate absolute number; we do not believe that is achievable at this data scale. The aim is to tell a chemist, before synthesis, which of two reasonable next steps is more likely to move potency without paying for it elsewhere.

The second part is a discipline rather than a method. Every design round will include a pre-registered prediction for each compound, recorded before synthesis and compared with the result afterward. Teams rarely do this, and we think that is why computational tools in medicinal chemistry earn so little trust: nobody keeps score. After four rounds across two series we will have a record of how often the models were right, where they failed, and whether they changed any decision.

The work will be done by a team of five at our institute, in close collaboration with the TB group in Durban, who will carry out the mouse studies. We budget for 480 synthesized compounds over three years. If the models help, we should see the median number of design cycles to reach a compound with MIC below 1 micromolar and mouse oral exposure above 10 micromolar-hours fall from the historical five to three or fewer. If they do not help, we will say so, and the scored dataset will still be a valuable resource for others.

Significance. Leishmaniasis is a neglected tropical disease that affects more than one million people each year, with the visceral form being fatal in the absence of treatment. In East Africa, where the burden is highest, patients depend on pentavalent antimonials and amphotericin B, whose use is limited by toxicity, cost and the need for hospitalisation. Miltefosine, the only oral drug, is teratogenic and shows decreasing efficacy in some regions. New oral drugs that are safe, affordable and effective are therefore urgently needed. However, investment from the private sector is minimal, and only a few academic laboratories in endemic countries have the means to perform drug discovery research on this disease.

Innovation. The present proposal combines three elements that, to our knowledge, have not been integrated before. First, we will use an open-source machine learning platform trained on public antileishmanial data to prioritise compounds from locally available natural product extracts and from synthetic libraries held by our partners in Ethiopia and Sudan. Second, we will generate the experimental data in endemic-country laboratories, which will reduce the dependency on external facilities. Third, we will return the experimental results to the models in an iterative cycle, so that the predictions improve with data that reflect local priorities.

Approach. In the first year, we will establish the intracellular amastigote assay in the laboratory at the University of Gondar, with the technical support of our collaborators at the Institute of Tropical Medicine in Antwerp, and we will validate the assay with reference drugs. In the second year, we will screen 600 compounds selected by the models, and we will confirm the dose-response of the hits against two clinical isolates of Leishmania donovani. Compounds with an EC50 below 5 micromolar and a selectivity index above 10 will proceed to preliminary ADME evaluation. In the third year, the best series will be optimised in cooperation with a medicinal chemistry partner, and the first in vivo efficacy experiments will be performed in a hamster model.

Expected outcomes. We expect to identify at least two new chemical series with antileishmanial activity, to train six local researchers in screening and data analysis, and to publish all data in open repositories. The project will build a sustainable platform that can be extended to other neglected diseases.

Background and Significance. Antimicrobial resistance is projected to cause 10 million deaths annually by 2050 if no action is taken, with the greatest burden falling on low- and middle-income countries.
