Gram-negative bacteria with carbapenem resistance have been designated critical priority pathogens by the World Health Organization, yet the clinical pipeline contains few agents active against them. A major barrier to progress is the difficulty of designing compounds that penetrate the Gram-negative envelope while avoiding efflux. Existing physicochemical guidelines are insufficient, and the experimental measurement of intracellular accumulation is labor intensive and low throughput.

Preliminary Data. In pilot work, we developed a random forest classifier trained on accumulation data for 297 compounds in Escherichia coli, obtained using LC-MS/MS quantification, which achieved a cross-validated accuracy of 78 percent. Analysis of feature importance indicated that the presence of a primary amine, low globularity, and a limited number of rotatable bonds were associated with high accumulation, in agreement with the eNTRy rules. Importantly, the model identified several exceptions, including three compounds lacking a primary amine that accumulated efficiently. These findings suggest that data-driven approaches can refine existing guidelines.

Research Approach. We propose to scale the accumulation assay to 3,000 compounds in three species, E. coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, using a miniaturized 96-well format and an automated sample preparation workflow that reduces the per-compound time from two days to four hours. We will then train multitask deep learning models to predict accumulation in each species, and will interpret them using attribution methods to derive design principles. The models will be validated prospectively by the synthesis of 60 analogues of a Gram-positive-only antibacterial scaffold, designed to improve Gram-negative activity.

Timeline and Milestones. Year 1 will focus on assay scale-up and the generation of the first 1,000 data points. In Year 2, we will complete data collection and develop the models. Year 3 will be dedicated to prospective validation and dissemination. Key milestones include a validated assay with a Z-prime above 0.6 by month 9, a model with AUROC above 0.85 by month 24, and at least 10 percent of designed analogues showing a four-fold improvement in Gram-negative MIC by month 33.

Impact. The data and models will be released openly, providing the community with the first large-scale resource of this type and enabling a more rational approach to the design of Gram-negative antibacterials.

Why this, and why us. Our group has maintained an open Python package for molecular standardization and featurization for nine years. It has about 300 regular users, several of whom run it in production inside companies that have never contributed a line of code or a dollar. That arrangement worked while the package was small. It is now at a point where one postdoc spends roughly half her time answering issues and fixing breakages caused by upstream changes, and this is the part of the work no one funds.

We are asking for support to put the package on a sustainable footing. The proposal does not promise new science in the usual sense. It promises that the tool our community uses to prepare data for machine learning will still run next year, on older laptops, with documentation that a first-year student can follow.

The work divides into three strands. The first is engineering: we will refactor the core to remove two heavy dependencies, move the test suite to continuous integration on three operating systems, and pin a compatibility matrix against the last four releases of RDKit. This is dull but takes about nine person-months. The second strand concerns users. We will run a series of six remote clinics with research groups in Nairobi, Lagos, Accra and Kampala, because our telemetry suggests that users there hit installation failures at about four times the rate of users in Europe. The third strand is governance. We will recruit four external maintainers, write down how decisions are made, and set up a small fund that pays contributors for review work, which tends to be where open-source projects run out of volunteers.

We will know the project has worked if median time to first successful run falls below fifteen minutes, if at least four maintainers outside our laboratory are merging changes by month eighteen, and if the proportion of issues closed within two weeks goes from 38 to 70 percent. We will publish these numbers every quarter, including when they are bad.

Specific Aims. The overall objective of this project is to identify host-directed antiviral compounds with broad-spectrum activity against arthropod-borne viruses, which cause recurrent outbreaks in tropical regions and for which no licensed antiviral treatment is available. We hypothesise that inhibition of host pyrimidine biosynthesis and of endosomal acidification represents a vulnerability shared by several flaviviruses and alphaviruses, and that approved drugs acting on these pathways can be repurposed with a favourable time to clinical evaluation.

Aim 1. To screen a library of 3,200 approved and clinical-stage compounds against dengue, Zika, Chikungunya and Mayaro viruses. We will use high-content imaging in human hepatoma and skin fibroblast cell lines, with automated quantification of infected cells and viability. Compounds that inhibit at least three of the four viruses with EC50 below 5 micromolar and a selectivity index above 10 will be considered broad-spectrum hits. Based on our preliminary experience, we expect to identify between 20 and 40 such compounds.

Aim 2. To define the mechanism of action of the broad-spectrum hits and to evaluate their combinations. Time-of-addition studies, uridine rescue experiments, and measurement of endosomal pH will be used to classify the compounds. Pairwise combinations of the most active compounds will be tested in a checkerboard design, and synergy will be calculated with the Bliss independence and Loewe additivity models. We will prioritise combinations that show synergy and that reduce the concentration of each drug below the clinically achievable plasma level.

Aim 3. To evaluate the efficacy of the best candidates in vivo. In collaboration with the animal facility at our partner institute, the most promising single agents and combinations will be tested in an interferon receptor-deficient mouse model of Zika and Chikungunya infection, with survival, viral load and clinical score as endpoints.

Significance and impact. This project follows a strategy that allows rapid translation, since the compounds have known safety profiles. Results will provide insight into host factors required by several viruses and may lead to therapeutic options for outbreak situations. All data will be made publicly available, and two PhD students from our country will be trained in antiviral screening, which will contribute to local preparedness for future epidemics.

Project Rationale. Generative models have demonstrated the ability to propose novel molecules with desired properties, but their application to neglected diseases has been limited by the scarcity of training data, the lack of constraints on synthetic cost, and the absence of rigorous experimental validation. This project will develop and evaluate a generative design platform tailored to the needs of drug discovery for Chagas disease and human African trypanosomiasis, in which compounds must be both active and inexpensive to manufacture.

Objective 1: Build a generative model conditioned on activity and synthetic cost. We will train a transformer-based model on 2.1 million bioactive molecules from ChEMBL and fine-tune it on 3,400 compounds with measured activity against Trypanosoma cruzi and Trypanosoma brucei. Generation will be guided by a multi-objective reward combining predicted potency, predicted selectivity, synthetic accessibility estimated by a retrosynthesis planner, and a cost proxy computed from building-block prices. We will compare the approach with three published baselines, including REINVENT and a diffusion-based method, using metrics that include chemist-rated acceptability, estimated cost per gram, and diversity.

Objective 2: Synthesize and test generated compounds. We will select 80 molecules representing diverse scaffolds and synthesize them using routes proposed by the planner and curated by medicinal chemists. Compounds will be tested in intracellular T. cruzi amastigote and T. brucei bloodstream form assays, together with cytotoxicity counter-screens. We define success as at least 10 compounds with EC50 below 1 micromolar and a selectivity index above 50, and at least three distinct scaffolds.

Objective 3: Establish an open platform. The code, trained models, generated molecules, and experimental results, including negative data, will be released through a public repository with documentation and a web interface. We will also organize two hackathons, one in Brazil and one in Argentina, to engage the local research community.

Innovation. The combination of cost-aware generation with experimental feedback from endemic-country laboratories is novel, and the release of negative results will provide valuable training data for the field. If successful, the platform could reduce the time and expense of early-phase discovery for diseases that receive little commercial investment.

Approach. A fair question about this proposal is why anyone should trust yet another ADMET model. The honest answer is that they should not, at first. The goal of the approach described below is to build the evidence that would justify trust, or show that it is unjustified.

We start from a collection of 1,200 compounds that our partners at the Drug Discovery Unit in Dundee and the H3D centre in Cape Town have profiled for solubility, microsomal stability, permeability and plasma protein binding, using the same protocols for the last five years. Most public ADMET data are assembled from papers that used different conditions and different units, which is where a lot of the apparent noise comes from. Our collection is smaller but consistent, and we will keep a quarter of it sealed until the end of the project.

Using the open data we will train a set of models, from simple fingerprint-based forests to a pretrained graph network, and make each predict the sealed compounds before anyone looks at the results. This is the part we care most about. We will also give the same task to a panel of ten medicinal chemists from five institutions, who will rank compounds by expected stability from structures alone. Chemists are not terrible at this, and a model that cannot beat a chemist on a quick look is not saving much time.

Then comes the prospective phase. For the final eighteen months, new compounds from three active malaria and tuberculosis series will be predicted before synthesis, and the predictions will be logged with a timestamp. When measurements arrive we will update a public scoreboard, showing for each endpoint how often the model, the chemists and a trivial baseline got the ranking right.

Risks are real. The consistent dataset might be too small for the endpoints we care about, and the models might do no better than chemists. Both outcomes would teach us where such tools should and should not be used, and that is a result worth funding.

Significance. Schistosomiasis is endemic in 78 countries and causes substantial morbidity, mainly in sub-Saharan Africa, where more than 90 percent of the people requiring treatment live. Control programmes depend on mass administration of praziquantel, a drug that does not prevent reinfection and shows low efficacy against immature worms. Because there is only one drug available, the development of resistance is a considerable risk. The discovery of new antischistosomal agents has been slow, in part because of the complexity of the parasite life cycle and the cost of in vivo experiments. Computational approaches could help to reduce these barriers, but they have been rarely applied to this disease, and the public data are limited.

Approach. We propose to establish a pipeline that combines transcriptomic analysis, target prediction and machine learning to prioritise compounds with antischistosomal activity. In the first phase, we will curate the existing data on activity against Schistosoma mansoni from the literature and from the open repositories, and we will complement it with new measurements of 500 compounds in adult worm and schistosomula assays performed in our laboratory. The new data will be used to train classification models based on molecular fingerprints and on predicted target profiles, using as targets the essential enzymes identified by RNA interference studies, such as thioredoxin glutathione reductase and histone deacetylase 8.

In the second phase, the models will be applied to screen virtual libraries including natural products from African medicinal plants, a source that is little explored and that has a long tradition in traditional treatment of the disease. The 150 top-ranked compounds will be tested in vitro, and active compounds with low cytotoxicity will be evaluated in a mouse model of infection in collaboration with our partner at the Swiss Tropical and Public Health Institute.

Training and sustainability. A central component of the proposal is the training of two doctoral students and three technicians in computational and experimental methods. We will organise an annual workshop for researchers from neighbouring countries, and the models will be released as open-source software with detailed documentation in English and French.

Expected results. We anticipate the identification of at least three new chemical classes with activity below 10 micromolar against adult worms, and a validated open resource for the community.

Resistance to artemisinin-based combination therapies has spread across the Greater Mekong subregion and is now being reported in several East African settings, which makes the search for chemically distinct antimalarials more urgent than ever. In this study we describe a phenotypic screen of 48,000 compounds drawn from a diversity-oriented library against chloroquine-resistant Plasmodium falciparum strain K1, with follow-up in a panel of multidrug-resistant field isolates. Of the primary hits, 212 compounds reduced parasite growth by more than 80 percent at 1 µM and showed no cytotoxicity against HepG2 cells at 10 µM. Clustering by scaffold grouped these hits into 37 chemotypes, and we prioritised six series with favourable physicochemical profiles for medicinal chemistry.

One series, a 2-aminopyridine-linked sulfonamide, retained potency against parasites carrying kelch13 mutations and showed a within-host half-life of approximately 9 hours in a humanised mouse model. Pharmacokinetic profiling of the lead series in rats revealed good oral exposure and moderate clearance, although plasma protein binding was high, which will need to be addressed in the next design cycle. Target deconvolution using resistance selection and thermal proteome profiling pointed to the cytochrome bc1 complex for two of the series, although the remaining hits appeared to act through mechanisms that will require further study.

These results identify tractable starting points for a lead optimisation campaign and illustrate how phenotypic screening combined with field-relevant parasite panels can keep the antimalarial pipeline supplied with mechanistically diverse candidates. We also observed that the phenotypic readout was sensitive to the choice of serum supplement, and we recommend that future screens report this variable explicitly so that results can be compared across laboratories. All screening data, including structures and dose-response curves, are deposited in an open repository to support reuse.

Carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae is a leading cause of hospital-acquired bloodstream infection, and wastewater surveillance has emerged as a complementary approach for tracking its circulation in the community. We analysed 312 influent samples collected weekly over 18 months from four wastewater treatment plants serving a metropolitan area of about 1.2 million residents, using a combination of selective culture, targeted qPCR for blaKPC, blaNDM and blaOXA-48, and short-read metagenomic sequencing of enriched concentrates. Carbapenemase gene signals were detected in 71 percent of samples, and their abundance correlated moderately with the number of clinical isolates reported by sentinel hospitals in the same catchments, with a lag of approximately two weeks.

Metagenomic assembly recovered 46 complete or near-complete plasmids, of which 19 carried blaKPC-2 on IncFII-type backbones that were nearly identical to plasmids isolated from patients admitted to two of the sentinel hospitals. Phylogenetic analysis of recovered K. pneumoniae sequence types revealed a dominant ST258 lineage together with several community-associated lineages not previously reported from clinical surveillance in the region. Our results suggest that wastewater monitoring can provide an early and population-wide signal of resistance gene dissemination, although the limited ability to link environmental signals to specific patients remains a constraint.

We discuss how such systems could be integrated into existing infection prevention programmes, and we outline the sampling frequency and sequencing depth needed to detect emerging lineages at useful lead times. Sampling every seven days was sufficient to capture the main temporal trends, but detecting low-abundance lineages required deeper sequencing than we had initially budgeted for.

Sequencing depth also mattered for the plasmid recovery. Plasmids below 20 kilobases were fragmented in most samples, so the counts reported here should be read as a lower bound on the diversity actually present in the catchment.

Tuberculosis remains the leading cause of death from a single infectious agent, and the emergence of extensively drug-resistant strains has made the identification of new chemical matter a priority for the field. In this work we report the hit-to-lead progression of a series of imidazo[1,2-a]pyridine-3-carboxamides identified from a whole-cell screen against Mycobacterium tuberculosis H37Rv. Starting from a hit with a minimum inhibitory concentration of 0.4 µM, we explored substitutions at three positions guided by a combination of matched molecular pair analysis and microsomal stability measurements. Modifications to the amide substituent improved potency against intracellular bacteria in macrophages by roughly an order of magnitude, while a fluorinated benzyl group reduced the rate of oxidative clearance in human liver microsomes from 62 to 14 µL per minute per milligram of protein.

The optimised compounds retained activity against a panel of 24 clinical isolates, including strains resistant to isoniazid, rifampicin and fluoroquinolones, and showed no cross-resistance with bedaquiline. In a murine model of chronic infection, the lead compound produced a reduction of 2.1 log10 colony-forming units in the lungs after four weeks of once-daily oral dosing at 25 mg/kg. hERG inhibition and cytochrome P450 liabilities remained the principal concerns, and we describe the structural changes that partly mitigated them.

Together these data define a lead series with a credible path toward preclinical development and highlight the value of integrating intracellular activity and metabolic stability early in tuberculosis drug discovery. Crystal structures of two analogues bound to the target, identified through a resistance selection experiment, are included as supplementary material, along with the full synthetic route and the complete profile of off-target screening data.

The synthetic route is short, with the key step being a single amide coupling that gave consistent yields across the series. This simplicity made it practical to explore the substitutions quickly, which in our hands was as important as the choice of scaffold.

We trained gradient-boosted and graph neural network models on roughly 28,000 measurements of aqueous solubility, Caco-2 permeability and human microsomal clearance drawn from public sources. Some of the sources disagree with each other. That was the first surprise. When we looked more closely, about one in eight compounds appeared in more than one dataset with values that differed by more than a log unit, and most of these discrepancies traced back to different assay conditions rather than to typos. We therefore cleaned the data by harmonising units and pH, dropping the most inconsistent records, and keeping the rest with a provenance flag.

The models were evaluated with scaffold-based splits, which are harsher than random splits and, in our experience, closer to what a medicinal chemist actually needs. Under this protocol, random forest models on extended connectivity fingerprints did almost as well as the graph networks, and the networks only pulled ahead for clearance, where three-dimensional features seemed to help. Performance on solubility was modest throughout (Spearman correlations between 0.55 and 0.63). Uncertainty estimates from a deep ensemble were informative enough to flag predictions that should not be trusted, and we measured how quickly accuracy degraded as compounds moved away from the training distribution.

Our main practical message is that a model's apparent accuracy depends heavily on how the data were split and cleaned, and that reporting both is more useful than reporting a single headline number. All code, curated datasets and split definitions are available openly.

We also tried a simple ridge regression as a sanity check. It performed worse than the forests on every endpoint, which was reassuring, since a linear baseline that matches the complex models would have pointed to a problem with the data rather than the architecture.

Visceral leishmaniasis still kills thousands of people each year in the Indian subcontinent and East Africa, and the drugs available to treat it are toxic, expensive or losing efficacy. We set out to test whether an existing library of kinase-focused compounds could yield starting points for a new oral treatment. The answer, at least partly, was yes. Of 1,900 compounds screened against intracellular Leishmania donovani amastigotes in macrophages, 58 showed selectivity indices above ten. Several of these belonged to a single chemotype that we had not expected to be active against trypanosomatids at all.

We followed up the best three chemotypes in a mouse model of visceral infection. One compound reduced liver parasite burden by about 70 percent after five daily doses, which is respectable but well short of what we would need. Pharmacokinetic work suggested that absorption was the limiting factor rather than metabolism, which points to formulation as a route to improvement. We are not yet sure whether the target is the parasite kinase we initially suspected or something else entirely; our proteomic data are ambiguous on that point.

This work is a reminder that neglected disease programmes often depend on repurposed libraries and modest budgets, and that the most useful outcome of a screen is sometimes a clear answer about what does not work. The compounds were also tested against promastigotes, where the activity profile was broadly similar, which suggests that the stage-specific effects we initially hoped for were not present in this chemotype. We have made the screening data public, including the inactive compounds, because they are as informative to future groups as the hits.

The dataset also includes a small number of compounds tested in duplicate across two independent laboratories. Agreement between the two sets was reasonable for potency but poor for selectivity, and we have flagged these records in the supplementary table so that readers can judge them for themselves.

When the first wave of interest in repurposing ran through the pandemic, the process looked simple: take an approved drug, test it against the virus, and see what sticks. Most of what stuck turned out to be nothing. We revisit that experience here with a systematic analysis of 412 clinical trials and 1,086 in vitro antiviral screens for SARS-CoV-2 and related coronaviruses, asking which drugs made it through and why most did not.

Two patterns stood out. First, compounds with cell-based activity at concentrations below 5 µM were rare, and nearly all of them were already known to inhibit host pathways such as the cathepsin or phosphatidylinositol kinase systems. Second, many early positives were artefacts of assay conditions, including high multiplicity of infection, plate-edge effects and cytotoxicity that masked viral signal. When we restricted the analysis to studies that reported dose-response curves and orthogonal confirmation, the number of credible candidates dropped sharply.

We then ran a computational pipeline that combined docking to viral proteases with a machine-learned activity model trained on those confirmed data. It recovered 9 of 11 known actives in a held-out set, but it also generated a long list of false positives that a chemist would find tempting. This is the honest state of the field. Repurposing can move quickly, yet it still depends on careful experiments and on the willingness to accept negative results. We argue that funders and journals should give the same weight to well-designed null screens as to headline hits. All computational outputs and the curated dataset are available with the paper.

Our curated list of trials was built from two registries and a manual search of published reports, and two reviewers independently classified each entry. Disagreements were resolved by discussion, and the final classification is provided with the supplementary data so that others can apply different criteria.

Open-source cheminformatics toolkits have become essential infrastructure for the drug discovery community, yet their documentation and testing practices are uneven, and many research groups still rely on proprietary software for tasks that could be done openly. In this paper we present a new release of an open toolkit for standardising, validating and featurising small molecules, which has been developed to address these gaps. The main novelty is a unified pipeline that performs salt stripping, tautomer canonicalisation, stereochemistry handling and charge neutralisation in a reproducible order, with every step documented and unit tested.

We evaluated the pipeline on five public benchmark collections totalling about 1.4 million structures and found that it produced identical canonical outputs for 99.6 percent of compounds when compared with a commercial standardiser, with the remaining differences arising mainly from ambiguous tautomers. Runtime was competitive, processing around 8,000 molecules per second on a single core. We also report a continuous integration setup that runs the full test suite against three Python versions and two operating systems, and a versioned set of expected outputs that allows users to verify their installation.

The toolkit is released under a permissive licence, and we describe how we have worked with contributors from several African universities to translate the documentation and to add examples relevant to local screening campaigns. We believe that open, well-tested tools lower the barrier to participation in computational chemistry, and we hope that this release will be useful both to experienced developers and to researchers who are just beginning to build their own pipelines.

Community feedback has shaped several recent changes, including clearer error messages for malformed input and a worked example for users who need to process large files in batches. We have kept these examples short so that new users can follow them without reading the full manual.

Capacity building in computational drug discovery across Africa has grown rapidly over the last decade, but the evaluation of these programmes has often been limited to counting workshops and participants. In this study we present a three-year assessment of a training and mentorship programme that paired early-career researchers from six countries with senior collaborators in Europe and in African institutions. We used a mixed-methods design, combining pre- and post-programme skills tests, structured interviews with 41 participants and analysis of research outputs including preprints, grant applications and software contributions.

Participants showed significant gains in the ability to write and run reproducible analysis scripts, and most reported that the mentorship component was more valuable than the taught modules. Within two years, 63 percent of participants had secured at least one external grant or fellowship, and 22 had contributed to open-source software projects used by groups outside their own institutions. We observed, however, that participants at institutions with limited access to high-performance computing were less likely to continue active research, which suggests that infrastructure remains a binding constraint.

Our findings support a model of capacity building that is long-term, locally led and attentive to the practical conditions in which researchers work. We discuss the implications for funders who wish to measure the impact of training beyond immediate satisfaction scores. Our approach combined a retrospective review of programme records with prospective follow-up, and we report response rates for each data source in the supplementary material.

Programme staff recorded attendance and the reasons for any missed sessions, which helped us separate logistical barriers from problems with content. Most absences were caused by competing teaching duties or unreliable internet access, and both factors are relevant to how the next cohort should be scheduled.

Generative models for molecular design have attracted considerable attention, but their evaluation remains inconsistent, and a generated library that looks chemically plausible is not necessarily useful for a specific therapeutic goal. Here we propose a framework for assessing recurrent and graph-based generative models that separates three questions: whether the generated molecules are valid and diverse, whether they resemble the training distribution in terms of physicochemical properties, and whether they satisfy a set of medicinal chemistry constraints defined in advance by the project team. We applied the framework to five architectures trained on a curated set of 600,000 drug-like compounds and used them to propose candidate inhibitors of a bacterial efflux pump.

Validity exceeded 98 percent for all models, but novelty and diversity varied considerably, and the best-performing model generated compounds that were synthetically accessible in 74 percent of cases according to a retrosynthesis-based score. After filtering for predicted activity and for the absence of structural alerts, 36 compounds were selected for purchase and testing, of which 4 showed measurable inhibition at 50 µM.

We reflect on what these numbers do and do not tell us. The hit rate is encouraging compared with random library screening, yet the sample is small, and the generated compounds were not optimised beyond the initial proposal. We recommend that future studies report the full evaluation protocol alongside any claims of discovery, and we release the code needed to reproduce our metrics.

Chemists in the partner laboratories reviewed a random sample of generated structures and rated their plausibility on a five-point scale. Their ratings agreed broadly with the automated metrics, although they were more critical of ring systems that the metrics had scored as acceptable. Two of the reviewers noted that several high-scoring compounds carried reactive groups that would be hard to justify in a medicinal chemistry programme, which is a reminder that the automated filters are only a first pass.

Malaria caused an estimated 597,000 deaths in 2023, with the great majority occurring in sub-Saharan Africa among young children. Although the disease has been in retreat for much of the past two decades, progress has stalled in several high-burden countries, and the spread of parasites with reduced susceptibility to artemisinin derivatives threatens to reverse the gains that have been made. Artemisinin partial resistance, mediated primarily by mutations in the kelch13 propeller domain, is now confirmed in multiple countries in East Africa and the Greater Mekong subregion, and partner drugs in artemisinin combination therapies are themselves beginning to show signs of failure. These developments have made the discovery of new antimalarials with novel mechanisms of action an urgent priority.

Drug discovery for malaria has historically relied on phenotypic screening against asexual blood-stage parasites, an approach that identified several clinically important compounds including the artemisinins themselves. Phenotypic campaigns have the advantage of selecting for whole-cell activity without requiring a validated target, but they also face challenges, including the difficulty of distinguishing true hits from compounds that act through general toxicity, and the challenge of deconvoluting mechanism once a hit has been identified. Target-based approaches have produced a number of validated candidates for the liver and transmission stages, yet they have been less productive for the blood stage in recent years.

In this context, the present work asks a narrower question: whether a diversity-oriented library, screened against a panel of field-derived parasites rather than a single laboratory strain, can yield chemically distinct series with activity against resistant isolates. We describe the screening strategy, the criteria used to prioritise compounds, and the first set of mechanistic experiments. Our aim is less to report a finished drug candidate than to show how a phenotypic pipeline can be designed to keep emerging resistance in view from the outset.

Antimicrobial resistance is responsible for a growing share of the global burden of bacterial infection, and the World Health Organization has identified several carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales as priority pathogens for which new treatments are urgently needed. Resistance is not confined to hospitals. Genes conferring resistance to last-resort antibiotics have been found in livestock, in surface water, and in municipal sewage, and the movement of these genes between environmental, animal and human reservoirs remains poorly understood. Effective surveillance is therefore a precondition for any strategy that aims to slow the spread of resistance, but conventional surveillance systems depend on clinical samples, which are collected unevenly and often too late to inform infection prevention.

Wastewater-based epidemiology offers a complementary route. Sewage integrates the faecal contributions of entire catchments, including people who never present to hospital, and it can be sampled at relatively low cost and high frequency. Previous work has shown that the abundance of antimicrobial resistance genes in wastewater correlates with antibiotic consumption and with clinical resistance rates, and metagenomic methods now make it possible to recover plasmids and strain-level signals from complex samples. Nevertheless, most studies have been short, have used a single method, or have not compared their findings with clinical data collected in parallel.

Here we report a longer and more systematic analysis of influent samples from four treatment plants serving a large metropolitan area. We combined targeted molecular detection with metagenomic sequencing and compared the resulting signals with the output of sentinel hospital laboratories over the same period. Our goal was to test whether wastewater can provide an early and population-wide indicator of carbapenemase circulation, and to identify the practical limits of such an approach.

Previous efforts to link wastewater signals to clinical data have relied on a single sentinel hospital or on monthly reporting, which limits the temporal resolution of any inference. The present study addresses both constraints, although not completely.

Tuberculosis treatment has changed more in the past fifteen years than in the previous four decades, with the introduction of bedaquiline, pretomanid and delamanid expanding options for drug-resistant disease. Yet the regimens built on these agents remain long, complex and burdened by adverse effects, and resistance to the newer drugs has already been documented in a small number of settings. The pipeline of compounds that are both chemically tractable and active against non-replicating bacteria is still thin, and most advanced candidates share mechanistic features with existing drugs, which limits their value in regimens where cross-resistance would be disastrous.

The hit-to-lead stage is where many tuberculosis programmes lose their most promising chemistry. Whole-cell hits often have adequate potency but poor metabolic stability, high lipophilicity or hERG liabilities that only become apparent after several rounds of chemistry. A recurring lesson from the field is that intracellular activity in macrophages, which better reflects the niche in which Mycobacterium tuberculosis persists in patients, is frequently lost during optimisation for extracellular potency. Assays that include this parameter early can therefore prevent expensive detours, but they add cost and complexity that many academic groups find difficult to sustain.

Our discussion of these results focuses on the imidazopyridine series as an example of how these trade-offs can be navigated. The compounds that retained intracellular activity were not the most potent in axenic culture, and their advantage became clear only when we measured both properties side by side. We suspect that similar comparisons across other series would reveal a broader pattern, and we encourage groups working on tuberculosis to report intracellular and extracellular data together. We also acknowledge that a single murine efficacy study is not sufficient to establish therapeutic value, and that the next phase will require pharmacokinetic and toxicology work that is considerably more demanding.

Our results suggest that a good deal of the apparent progress in ADMET prediction is sensitive to evaluation choices that are easy to overlook. Random splits, which remain common, allow models to exploit near-duplicate chemistry and therefore overstate their usefulness for compounds that are structurally new. When we moved to scaffold splits, the gap between sophisticated architectures and simple fingerprint-based forests narrowed considerably. That does not mean graph networks are not worth using. It means that their advantage has to be shown under conditions that resemble the decisions a team actually makes.

The data cleaning step probably matters more than we initially assumed. Solubility measurements are notoriously sensitive to buffer, temperature and the method used to reach equilibrium, and a model trained on a mixture of these conditions learns partly to predict the laboratory rather than the molecule. We kept provenance flags for this reason, and we would encourage other groups to do the same. A model that knows where its labels came from can be used more sensibly than one that treats every number as equally reliable.

Uncertainty estimates were useful, though not uniformly so. The deep ensemble flagged the most extreme predictions well, but it was less helpful in the middle of the range, where errors were large and the uncertainty was not. We think this is a general limitation of current approaches rather than something specific to our models. Users should treat uncertainty as a rough guide to where caution is needed, not as a calibrated probability. Finally, the models are only as good as the chemistry they have seen. Several of the compounds our users care about sit outside the applicability domain of the public data, and for these the honest answer is that the model cannot say much. We think this should be stated plainly in every tool that offers predictions to non-specialists.

The leishmaniasis result was more mixed than we had hoped, and we think it is worth saying so directly. A compound that clears most of the parasite burden in a short course of dosing is the kind of finding that tends to attract attention, but our best molecule needed a higher dose than is realistic for an oral drug aimed at low-income patients, and its exposure data pointed to absorption problems that medicinal chemistry alone may not fix.

We also want to be cautious about the mechanism. The kinase we first suspected did not show the expected changes in our proteomic experiments, and the one signal that did emerge came from a protein whose role in parasite biology is not well characterised. It is possible that the active compounds hit several targets, which is common among kinase-directed scaffolds, but it is equally possible that our assay conditions favoured a particular type of response. Without a resistance selection experiment, we cannot say which.

There is a broader point about how neglected disease research is organised. Much of the useful work in this area happens in small teams that cannot afford to run every follow-up experiment, and the results of screens that did not produce a clear hit rarely reach the literature. Publishing the inactive compounds and the full dose-response data was a deliberate choice, and we would encourage other groups to make similar decisions, since a shared record of what did not work saves time for everyone. Finally, the mouse model, while standard, may not predict human response well for this infection, and we would not want the reported efficacy to be read as more than an encouraging early result. The real test will be whether a reformulated compound can achieve adequate exposure in larger animals before it is considered for clinical work.

The repurposing literature from the pandemic contains a lot of useful information, but it is also full of results that were never meant to last. Our analysis suggests that the field would have benefited from stricter reporting standards from the beginning. Many early studies reported single-dose inhibition at concentrations far above what could be reached in plasma, and some relied on cell lines that lack the transporters responsible for drug uptake in human lung tissue. These are not subtle problems, and they are easy to fix, yet they persisted for months because the pressure to publish quickly was intense.

We do not think repurposing is a dead end. Some of the candidates that did survive careful testing, particularly host-directed agents that modulate endosomal entry, remain interesting and may be useful against related viruses that are not yet on the radar of most funders. The difficulty is that the screening economics do not favour exploring these options systematically. A library of approved drugs is cheap to test, but confirming activity requires dose-response work, orthogonal assays and, ideally, some understanding of the pharmacokinetics in the relevant tissue. That work is slow, and it does not generate the kind of headline that attracts follow-on funding.

Our computational pipeline added little beyond what the best experimental data already told us, which is perhaps the most important finding in this section. Docking to viral proteases produced many attractive poses, but the correlation with measured activity was weak once compounds with similar scaffolds were considered together. A machine-learned model did better, but only because it was trained on data that had already been cleaned by hand. For that reason we would recommend that future repurposing efforts be organised around a predefined set of criteria for activity, a commitment to publishing negative results, and an early plan for pharmacokinetic validation. None of this is novel. It is simply what good screening looked like before the emergency began, and it is what the next emergency will require.

The results of our benchmarking show that the pipeline is reliable for most common cases, but we should be honest about the remaining differences. Most of the disagreements with the commercial standardiser concern tautomers, where the choice of canonical form depends on conventions that are not universally agreed. We have documented these choices and made them configurable, which is the best we can do without imposing one convention on all users. It is important to note that a standardiser that matches a particular commercial product is not automatically correct, and users should check their own use cases.

Another issue is maintenance. Open-source projects of this kind depend on a small number of contributors, and the sustainability of the code is a matter of ongoing concern. We have tried to reduce this risk by writing extensive tests, by keeping the codebase modular, and by including the expected outputs in the repository so that new contributors can check their changes. However, these measures do not replace funding for maintenance, and the community has not yet found a reliable way to pay for the work that keeps these tools running.

The collaboration with African universities taught us that documentation is not a translation exercise alone. Examples that are relevant to local screening campaigns, such as those involving antimalarial and antitubercular chemotypes, were more useful to our partners than generic examples drawn from pharmaceutical datasets. It also became clear that installation on shared computing clusters with restricted permissions required additional guidance, which we have now added to the documentation. We hope that this work encourages groups to share their pipelines openly, and to treat testing and reproducibility as part of the scientific output rather than as an afterthought. Open infrastructure is not free to build or maintain, but it reduces the need for every laboratory to reinvent the same basic steps.

The findings of this evaluation should be read with the context of the programme in mind. The mentorship model depended on sustained time from senior collaborators, which is not always available, and the success of individual pairings varied considerably. Some mentees reported that their mentors were very responsive and helped them to develop independent projects, while others described long periods with little contact. We think that structured expectations, such as regular written milestones and shared project plans, were the factor most associated with positive outcomes, although our sample was too small to test this formally.

Our results also show that capacity is not only a matter of individual skills. Participants who returned to institutions with supportive leadership and access to basic computing resources were more likely to maintain their research activity. Those who did not often found that the skills they had acquired were difficult to apply in their own settings, and some left academia altogether. This suggests that training programmes should be designed together with the institutions that will receive the trainees, and that funders should consider support for infrastructure as part of the same investment.

It is also important to recognise that the programme itself was shaped by the funding priorities of its donors, and that the choice of topics reflected a particular view of what African research should look like. Participants were asked about their priorities, and several said that they wanted more emphasis on epidemiology and health systems research, which the programme had not fully addressed. We are grateful for this feedback and have incorporated it into the next cycle. Finally, we note that counting outputs such as grants and software contributions is useful but incomplete. These measures capture some of what happened, but they do not capture the confidence participants felt, the networks they built, or the younger researchers they went on to teach. We have begun a longer follow-up that aims to include these dimensions, and we hope that others evaluating similar programmes will do the same.

Our evaluation framework is deliberately modest in its claims. It does not tell us whether a generated molecule will be active in a living organism, and it does not replace the judgement of a medicinal chemist who can see the proposed structures and consider their practical value. What it does provide is a consistent way to ask whether a model is producing chemistry that is plausible, varied and aligned with the constraints that a project team has specified. In our view this is a necessary step before any generative model is used to propose compounds for synthesis, and it is a step that many published studies have skipped.

The hit rate we observed, around 11 percent of purchased compounds in the primary assay, should be interpreted cautiously. The sample of 36 compounds is small, and the selection process involved filters that themselves affect the outcome. Comparing our result with random screening is informative but not decisive, because random libraries of commercial compounds have their own biases. We would prefer to see prospective comparisons in which generated and conventional candidates are selected by the same criteria and tested in parallel.

We also observed that novelty and synthetic accessibility were in tension. The models that generated the most novel structures tended to propose compounds that were harder to make, while the more conservative models produced molecules that were easier to obtain but closer to known chemistry. Deciding which trade-off is acceptable depends on the project stage, and we think that generative models should be presented with explicit statements of this trade-off rather than with a single aggregate score. Finally, the code and metrics are released so that others can test whether our conclusions hold on different targets and datasets. We expect that some of our observations will not generalise, and we would welcome the replication effort.

This manuscript reports a phenotypic screen for antimalarial compounds against chloroquine-resistant P. falciparum, followed by activity testing against field isolates and a preliminary mechanistic analysis. The authors identify several chemotypes with submicromolar potency and suggest that one series acts through the cytochrome bc1 complex. The topic is important, the screening panel is a welcome addition to the field, and the paper is generally well written. My overall impression is that the work is a useful contribution but that several claims need to be supported more carefully before publication.

The main strength of the study is the use of a field-relevant parasite panel alongside the laboratory strain. This gives the reader some confidence that the hits are not simply exploiting features of a single adapted line. The scaffold analysis is clear, and the authors are candid about the proportion of hits that remain mechanistically unexplained. The pharmacokinetic data for the lead series are a good addition, even if preliminary.

My principal concern is the target assignment. The thermal proteome profiling data are presented as supporting the cytochrome bc1 hypothesis for two series, but the figure showing shifts in melting temperature is difficult to interpret without the replicate data, and the authors do not report how many proteins passed the significance threshold. I would ask for the full dataset, a description of the statistical model, and a resistance selection experiment with whole-genome sequencing of the selected lines. Without these, the mechanism should be described as tentative. Second, the cytotoxicity measurements were performed at a single concentration. For a compound class that the authors hope to advance, a dose-response curve against at least two mammalian cell lines is necessary. Third, the statement that the lead series showed a half-life of nine hours should be accompanied by the number of animals and the confidence interval.

Minor points. The abbreviation SI is used before it is defined. Figure 3 would benefit from a legend that explains the colour scale. The supplementary tables should include the InChIKeys for all compounds to allow reproduction.

The authors present a wastewater surveillance study of carbapenemase genes in influent from four treatment plants over eighteen months. They combine targeted qPCR, metagenomic sequencing and comparison with sentinel hospital data. The central claim is that wastewater signals lead clinical reports by about two weeks and that recovered plasmids are closely related to those isolated from patients. The question is important and the dataset is substantial, so the manuscript has the potential to make a valuable contribution to surveillance methodology.

The principal strength is the length and frequency of sampling, which allows the authors to examine temporal relationships rather than making cross-sectional comparisons. The plasmid analysis is carefully done, and the use of near-identity thresholds to link environmental and clinical sequences is appropriate. I also appreciated the honest treatment of limitations in the discussion.

My concerns relate mainly to the lag analysis. The authors report a correlation of approximately two weeks, but the method used to estimate the lag is not described in enough detail to judge whether the result is robust. I would ask them to state the cross-correlation procedure, report confidence intervals, and show whether the lag persists when hospital admissions rather than isolate counts are used as the clinical comparator. Some of the sentinel hospitals changed their reporting practice during the study period, and this should be addressed. A second concern is the assumption that all sequenced plasmids reflect circulation in the catchment. Sewage can carry material from outside the catchment, and the authors should discuss how they excluded plasmids that might originate from a different source population. Third, the sequence type analysis relies on assemblies from short reads, which may be fragmented; the authors should report assembly quality for the lineages they emphasise.

Minor points include inconsistent use of the terms carbapenemase and carbapenemase-producing, a missing reference for the qPCR primer design, and a figure whose axis labels are too small to read when printed.

This manuscript describes the hit-to-lead optimisation of a series of imidazopyridine carboxamides against Mycobacterium tuberculosis. The authors report improved intracellular activity, reduced microsomal clearance, activity against clinical isolates with diverse resistance profiles, and a modest reduction in bacterial load in a murine chronic infection model. The work addresses a real need, and the combination of intracellular and extracellular assays is a strength. I think the manuscript could be publishable in a good journal after revision, but several issues need attention.

The most convincing part of the paper is the structure-activity analysis. The authors have clearly explored the chemical space around the hit in a systematic way, and the matched molecular pair analysis is presented clearly. The inclusion of clinical isolates with resistance to isoniazid, rifampicin and fluoroquinolones is valuable, and the absence of cross-resistance with bedaquiline is an interesting observation that deserves more emphasis.

My major concern is the in vivo efficacy experiment. A single study with four weeks of dosing and a reduction of 2.1 log10 colony-forming units is presented as evidence of therapeutic potential, but the manuscript does not include the number of animals per group, the randomisation procedure, or the blinding of the plate counts. The comparison group receiving the standard regimen is not clearly defined, and it is unclear whether the dose of the reference drugs was matched to published exposures. These details are essential for interpreting the result. Second, the hERG data are reported as an IC50 without a description of the assay format or the positive control. Given that hERG liability was one of the central problems in the series, the authors should present the full dose-response curves and discuss how the structural changes affected the margin relative to predicted free plasma concentrations. Third, the crystal structures are mentioned but not shown in the main text. If they support the proposed binding mode, they should be included with the relevant electron density maps.

Minor points: the synthetic route in the supplementary material lacks yields for several intermediates, and the naming of compounds switches between two conventions in the text and tables.

I read this manuscript with real interest, because the question it asks is one that every group building ADMET models eventually runs into. The authors compare several architectures on solubility, permeability and clearance, using scaffold splits and a careful cleaning procedure. Their conclusion that simpler models are competitive under harder evaluation is, in my view, the most useful message of the paper. I have some reservations, which I set out below, but I think the work deserves publication after revision.

What I liked most is the attention to data provenance. The authors noticed that the same compounds appear in multiple sources with conflicting values, and rather than averaging these numbers they flagged the disagreement and tested whether it affected model performance. This is the kind of detail that is often skipped, and it is the reason I trust the headline comparisons more than I otherwise would. The uncertainty analysis is also thoughtful, and the deep ensemble results are presented honestly, including the places where they do not help.

My main concern is with the statistical comparison. The differences between random forests and graph networks on solubility are small, and the paper reports them without confidence intervals or any test of significance across the five random seeds. I would like to see bootstrap intervals over the test compounds and some indication of whether the ranking is stable across the three scaffold split definitions. Without this, the claim that the networks only pull ahead for clearance is suggestive rather than established. I am also not convinced that the applicability domain analysis goes far enough. The authors show that error increases as compounds move away from the training distribution, which is expected, but they do not indicate how many of the compounds in their intended application would fall outside that domain. A short table of this would help readers judge how far the models can be trusted.

Minor points: the Spearman correlations in the abstract should be given with their intervals, the hyperparameter search space should be listed in full, and the code repository should include the exact versions of the cheminformatics libraries used.

This is a careful and honest paper about a screen against intracellular Leishmania donovani. The authors found a chemotype with selectivity and showed modest efficacy in a mouse model of visceral infection. They are upfront that the mechanism is unclear and that the lead compound would need substantial work before it could be considered as a drug. I appreciated that tone. My recommendation is minor revision, mainly because the in vivo section needs clearer reporting and the mechanistic claims need to be toned down.

The screen itself is well designed. Using intracellular amastigotes in macrophages rather than promastigotes is the right choice, and the inclusion of inactive compounds in the supplementary data is valuable. The selectivity index is computed against a relevant mammalian cell type, and the authors have reported the cytotoxicity data for all hits.

The in vivo experiment is my main concern. Liver parasite burden is reduced by about 70 percent after five daily doses, but the manuscript does not state whether the reduction was compared with vehicle-treated animals in the same experiment, nor does it give the number of mice per group or the parasite quantification method. The pharmacokinetic data suggest poor absorption, and I would like to see the exposure values alongside the efficacy results so that readers can judge whether the efficacy was achieved at a plausible concentration. On the target question, the proteomic data are described as ambiguous, which is fair, but the discussion sometimes reads as if the kinase hypothesis was supported. I would suggest rewording these passages so that the evidence is presented as preliminary. A resistance selection experiment would help a great deal, and if it is not feasible, the authors should say so explicitly.

Minor points: the figure legends repeat information from the main text, the dosing schedule should be given in a table, and the spelling of the parasite species is inconsistent in the references.

This manuscript offers a retrospective analysis of antiviral repurposing studies for coronaviruses, combined with a computational pipeline for prioritising candidates. The authors argue that many early positives were artefacts and that stricter reporting would have saved the field considerable effort. I think the first part of the argument is correct and well supported. The second part, the computational pipeline, is less convincing and I would ask the authors to either strengthen it substantially or reduce its prominence.

The systematic analysis of 1,086 in vitro screens is the paper's strongest contribution. The authors have assembled a dataset that many people would find useful, and their classification of studies by assay quality is transparent. The observation that multiplicity of infection and plate-edge effects inflated apparent activity is convincing, and the figure showing how the number of credible candidates falls when these studies are excluded is effective.

My concerns focus on the modelling. The docking scores are reported as if they provide meaningful discrimination, but the correlation with activity across compounds with different scaffolds is weak, as the authors partly acknowledge. The machine-learned model recovers nine of eleven known actives, but the test set is very small, and it is not clear whether the training data overlapped with the test compounds through analogues. I would ask for a scaffold-based evaluation and a clearer description of how the false positives were handled. I would also like the authors to say more about the clinical trial data. The analysis treats trial outcomes as evidence about the antiviral activity of drugs, but many trials were underpowered or confounded by background therapy. A short discussion of these limitations would make the conclusions more balanced.

Minor points: the abbreviation MOI should be defined, the search strategy in the methods should list the databases and date ranges, and the reference list contains several preprints that have since been published and should be updated.

The manuscript describes a new release of an open-source toolkit for molecular standardisation, with validation against a commercial standardiser and a continuous integration framework. The software is useful, the documentation is generally good, and the authors have made a commendable effort to involve researchers from African institutions. I recommend acceptance after minor revision. My comments are intended to help the authors strengthen the paper and make the comparisons more informative for potential users.

The main strength of the manuscript is its focus on reproducibility. The authors provide a versioned set of expected outputs, which allows users to verify their installation, and they run the test suite across multiple Python versions and operating systems. These are practices that many software papers in our field do not follow, and the authors deserve credit for them. The runtime comparison is also helpful, since performance is a real constraint for users who process large libraries.

My principal concern is the benchmark. The claim that the pipeline matches the commercial standardiser for 99.6 percent of compounds is presented without a breakdown of the disagreements by category. Since the differences are said to arise mainly from ambiguous tautomers, the authors should report how many compounds are affected in each dataset, and whether the disagreement is concentrated in particular chemical classes. It would also help to know which tautomer convention the commercial tool follows, because a reader cannot judge whether the difference reflects an error in one tool or simply a different choice. I also wonder about maintenance. The paper mentions a small number of core contributors, and the authors should say more about how the project will be supported over the next several years, including whether any institutional commitments exist.

Minor points: the description of the salt stripping rules should cite the source of the list of counter-ions, the table of runtimes should give the hardware specification, and the phrase unit tested should be replaced with covered by unit tests in the methods section for clarity.

This is a useful and humane evaluation of a training and mentorship programme in computational drug discovery. The authors have collected both quantitative and qualitative data, they report the outcomes honestly, and they do not overclaim. I think the paper is a valuable addition to a literature that often measures the wrong things. My concerns are mostly about the design and the reporting of the mixed methods, and I believe they can be addressed in a revision.

The strongest aspect is the decision to follow participants for two years and to look at outputs beyond satisfaction surveys. Counting grants, preprints and software contributions is an imperfect measure, but it is more informative than the usual workshop headcounts, and the authors make clear what it does and does not capture. The interviews are also rich, and the quotations that illustrate the role of mentorship are vivid without being sentimental.

My main concern is the sample. Forty-one interviews is a reasonable number for qualitative work, but the paper does not describe how the interviewees were selected, and it is possible that people who had good outcomes were more willing to talk. The authors should state the response rate, describe any attempt to include participants who left research, and discuss how this might bias the findings. The claim that infrastructure is a binding constraint rests on a comparison of participants at institutions with and without high-performance computing access. I found this comparison suggestive but not conclusive, because institutions differ in many ways. The authors should be more careful in the abstract and conclusions about the causal language used.

Minor points: the summary table should include the number of mentors per cohort, the interview guide should be provided as supplementary material, and the discussion of funder priorities could be expanded slightly to explain how topics were chosen.

The authors propose an evaluation framework for generative models of molecules and apply it to five architectures with a prospective test on an efflux pump target. The motivation is sound. Many papers in this area report validity and novelty without relating them to the decisions a project team actually makes, and the separation of questions into validity, distribution similarity and project constraints is helpful. I recommend major revision, because the prospective component is too small to support the strength of the conclusions as currently written.

The framework itself is clear and its components are well motivated. The use of a retrosynthesis-based score for synthetic accessibility is an improvement over simpler heuristics, and releasing the code for the metrics is commendable. The authors have also been appropriately careful about describing their evaluation as a first attempt rather than a definitive method.

My major concern is the experimental test. Thirty-six compounds were selected from the generated set and tested at a single concentration, with four showing measurable inhibition. The manuscript then compares this rate with random library screening, but the comparison is not controlled. The selection criteria included filters for predicted activity and structural alerts, which means that the generated compounds were pre-enriched by the authors' own pipeline. I would ask the authors either to include a comparison in which conventional candidates are selected by the same criteria, or to present the prospective result as a pilot rather than as evidence of superiority. A second concern is the tension between novelty and synthetic accessibility. The authors note this trade-off but do not quantify it across models. A plot showing both properties for all architectures would make the trade-off visible and help readers judge which model is most suitable for their own stage of work.

Minor points: the definition of diversity should be stated mathematically, the training set curation should indicate how duplicates were removed, and the figures would benefit from a consistent colour scheme across architectures.

Specific Aim 1 is to identify and prioritise chemically distinct antiplasmodial series from a diversity-oriented library of 48,000 compounds, using a phenotypic screen against chloroquine-resistant P. falciparum and a panel of six multidrug-resistant field isolates collected in Uganda and Cambodia. Hits will be defined as compounds with IC50 below 1 µM and selectivity indices above 50 relative to HepG2 cells. We will cluster hits by scaffold and prioritise up to six series based on potency across the field panel, physicochemical properties and early metabolic stability. This aim will produce a ranked list of series with complete dose-response data and a publicly deposited dataset.

Specific Aim 2 is to determine the mechanism of action of the prioritised series. We will generate resistance in the laboratory by stepwise selection, sequence the selected lines to identify candidate targets, and validate these using thermal proteome profiling and, where appropriate, recombinant enzyme assays. We anticipate that at least two series will act through the cytochrome bc1 complex or a related respiratory component, but the remaining series may act through unknown mechanisms, and we will allocate effort accordingly. The deliverable for this aim is a mechanistic classification of each series with supporting data.

Specific Aim 3 is to advance the best series into lead optimisation with a focus on oral exposure, plasma protein binding and activity against kelch13-mutant parasites. Medicinal chemistry will proceed in two cycles of design, synthesis and testing, supported by pharmacokinetic studies in rodents. Success will be defined as a lead compound with an in vitro IC50 below 100 nM against resistant isolates, a within-host half-life greater than eight hours in mice, and no cytotoxicity at 10 µM. Significance: artemisinin partial resistance is now confirmed in East Africa and the Greater Mekong subregion, and the pipeline of mechanistically novel antimalarials remains thin. This project will supply new starting points tested against the parasites that matter for treatment failure, and all data will be shared openly.

Specific Aim 1 is to establish a longitudinal wastewater surveillance system for carbapenemase genes across four treatment plants serving the metropolitan catchment, with weekly sampling for 24 months. We will quantify blaKPC, blaNDM and blaOXA-48 by targeted qPCR, recover K. pneumoniae isolates by selective culture, and perform shotgun metagenomic sequencing on concentrated samples at a depth of 20 million reads. The deliverable will be a standardised dataset that links gene abundance, sequence type and plasmid structure to sampling date and plant.

Specific Aim 2 is to compare wastewater signals with clinical surveillance. We will obtain anonymised isolate data from sentinel laboratories in the same catchments and estimate the temporal relationship between wastewater abundance and clinical isolate counts using cross-correlation and distributed lag models. We will test whether the lead time is stable across seasons and whether it is affected by changes in hospital reporting practice. The primary outcome is the estimated lag and its confidence interval.

Specific Aim 3 is to identify plasmids and lineages that move between hospital and community reservoirs. We will assemble plasmids from metagenomic data, compare them with clinical plasmids using a near-identity threshold, and assess whether shared plasmids cluster in time and place. We will report assembly quality for each lineage and the proportion of signals that could plausibly originate outside the catchment. Significance: resistance to last-line antibiotics is increasing, and clinical surveillance alone reaches patients too late to inform infection prevention. A wastewater system that provides a population-wide, early indicator would give health authorities a practical tool. The methods will be published openly to support replication in other regions.

Budget and staffing are described in the attached justification. Sampling and sequencing costs are modest relative to the value of an early warning system, and the largest single item is the bioinformatics support needed to maintain the analysis pipeline across the full project period.

Specific Aim 1 is to complete the hit-to-lead optimisation of the imidazo[1,2-a]pyridine-3-carboxamide series with the goal of identifying a preclinical candidate. We will synthesise approximately 180 analogues guided by matched molecular pair analysis and microsomal stability data, with compounds prioritised on intracellular activity in THP-1 macrophages, activity against a panel of 24 clinical isolates and predicted hERG margin. The primary outcome will be a candidate with an intracellular minimum inhibitory concentration below 0.5 µM, human microsomal clearance below 15 µL per minute per milligram, and a hERG IC50 at least 30-fold above the predicted free plasma concentration.

Specific Aim 2 is to define the mechanism of action and resistance profile of the lead series. We will select resistant mutants under drug pressure, perform whole-genome sequencing, and confirm candidate targets by overexpression and by crystallography of the compound bound to the protein. These experiments will determine whether the series shares a mechanism with existing agents and will guide the design of combination studies.

Specific Aim 3 is to evaluate efficacy in a murine model of chronic tuberculosis infection. Groups of mice will receive the candidate alone or in combination with a standard regimen for four weeks, with bacterial burden measured by colony counts in lungs and spleen. Animal numbers have been calculated using a power analysis for a detectable difference of 1.5 log10 colony-forming units. Significance: tuberculosis still kills more people than any other single infectious agent, and drug-resistant strains limit treatment options. A new series with activity against non-replicating and intracellular bacteria, and no cross-resistance with current agents, would address a clear gap.

The medicinal chemistry team will work closely with the pharmacology group, and go/no-go decisions at the end of each cycle will be made by a joint committee with an external advisor. This structure is intended to stop programmes that are not improving, rather than to continue them by default.

We want to be direct about what this project will and will not do. Specific Aim 1 is to build a curated, provenance-annotated dataset of solubility, permeability and clearance measurements from public sources, with conflicting measurements flagged rather than averaged. We expect the final dataset to contain around 30,000 records. The curation rules will be written before any modelling begins and will be published with the data. This matters more than it sounds: our pilot work suggested that roughly one compound in eight has conflicting values across sources, and models trained on unflagged data learn partly to predict laboratory conditions.

Specific Aim 2 is to compare model architectures under scaffold-based evaluation. We will train random forests, gradient-boosted trees and graph neural networks, and evaluate them with three scaffold split definitions and five random seeds. Results will be reported with bootstrap confidence intervals. Our hypothesis is that simple fingerprint models will be competitive for solubility, while three-dimensional features may help for clearance. If that hypothesis is wrong, we will say so.

Specific Aim 3 is to quantify applicability domain and uncertainty. We will use deep ensembles and distance-based measures to flag predictions outside the training distribution, and we will test how well these flags identify large errors on held-out compounds. The deliverable will be a tool that reports predictions together with a plain statement of confidence. Significance: medicinal chemists rely on these models every day, yet the evaluation practices in the literature often overstate performance. A transparent, well-documented benchmark will help teams decide when a model is worth using.

Data and code will be deposited in a public repository with a version tag for each release, and all model cards will be generated automatically from the same evaluation scripts so that reported numbers can be reproduced without manual transcription.

Visceral leishmaniasis is fatal if untreated, and the available drugs are toxic, costly or threatened by resistance. This project will test whether a kinase-focused library can yield an oral treatment candidate. Specific Aim 1 is to confirm activity and selectivity for the nineteen best chemotypes identified in our primary screen, using intracellular L. donovani amastigotes in primary macrophages and a panel of mammalian cell lines for toxicity. We will report full dose-response curves and publish the results, including negative data.

Specific Aim 2 is to address the mechanism question directly. Our current proteomic data are ambiguous, and we do not yet know whether the active compounds act on a parasite kinase, on a host pathway or on something else. We will generate resistant parasites where possible, sequence them, and test candidate targets using knockdown and recombinant assays. If the mechanism remains unclear after these experiments, we will say so and will not claim a target we cannot support.

Specific Aim 3 is to improve oral exposure in the most promising chemotype. Pilot pharmacokinetic work suggests that absorption, rather than metabolism, limits exposure. We will test formulation options and two rounds of structural modification aimed at solubility, and we will measure exposure in mice and, for the final candidate, in a larger species. Efficacy will be assessed in the hamster model, which better reflects human visceral disease than the mouse model we used previously. Significance: few groups work on this disease with open data and modest budgets. The project will produce both a candidate and a public record of what did not work, which we believe is of practical value to others in the field.

The project team includes a veterinarian with experience in hamster infection models and a pharmacokineticist who has worked on formulation for low-income settings. Their involvement is central to the feasibility of the in vivo work, which would otherwise be outside our current expertise.
