The pandemic showed how quickly repurposing studies can generate attractive results, and how many of those results fail under careful testing. This proposal aims to build a repurposing pipeline that is slower and more rigorous, with decisions made in advance rather than after the data arrive. Specific Aim 1 is to assemble a curated dataset of antiviral screening results against coronaviruses and related viruses, classifying each study by assay quality, including multiplicity of infection, dose-response design and orthogonal confirmation. We will use this dataset to define a standard for what counts as a credible candidate.

Specific Aim 2 is to test a set of approved drugs and host-directed agents against three viruses in a predefined panel, with full dose-response data and cytotoxicity measured in relevant human cell types, including primary airway epithelium. Compounds will be selected from the curated literature and from a library of approved drugs, with the selection criteria fixed before testing begins. We expect most compounds to fail, and we will report those failures in full.

Specific Aim 3 is to determine whether computational prioritisation adds value beyond the experimental data. We will compare docking and a machine-learned activity model against the Aim 2 results, using scaffold-based evaluation and a predefined threshold for success. If neither method outperforms a simple baseline, we will report that finding and recommend against using such methods for prioritisation in this setting. Significance: repurposing remains one of the few fast routes to new antiviral options, but it depends on the quality of the evidence. This project will establish a transparent standard and will publish negative results as openly as positive ones.

Biosafety and regulatory requirements for work with live coronaviruses will be met through an established containment facility, and all protocols will be reviewed by the institutional committee before experiments begin. Timelines for these approvals have been included in the work plan.

The aim of this project is to maintain and extend an open-source toolkit for molecular standardisation and featurisation, which is currently used by several research groups across Europe, Africa and Latin America. Specific Aim 1 is to strengthen the test suite and documentation so that the toolkit can be installed and verified on shared computing clusters with restricted permissions. We will add expected-output tests for ten additional benchmark datasets, write installation guides for three common cluster environments, and translate the main documentation into French and Portuguese with the help of partner institutions.

Specific Aim 2 is to make the tautomer and stereochemistry conventions transparent and configurable. At present, users cannot easily see which convention the pipeline applies, and disagreements with commercial tools are difficult to diagnose. We will publish a detailed comparison of conventions, add configuration options with documented defaults, and provide a report that lists which compounds change under each option. This will allow users to choose the behaviour that matches their own research standards.

Specific Aim 3 is to establish a sustainable governance model. Our current maintenance depends on a small number of contributors, which is a risk for any tool used by groups that cannot easily fund software development. We will set up a steering group with members from partner institutions, define contribution guidelines and a release schedule, and explore institutional commitments for ongoing support. The deliverable will be a published governance document and at least two maintainers from outside the founding group. Significance: open infrastructure lowers the barrier to computational chemistry, but only if it remains maintained and documented. This proposal responds directly to requests from users in settings where commercial software is not affordable.

Training materials will be designed with partner institutions and tested in workshops held in two countries, with feedback used to revise the documentation before each release. Participants who complete the training will be invited to join the steering group as contributors.

This proposal requests support for the second phase of a mentorship programme in computational drug discovery, building on the evaluation of the first cohort. The programme pairs early-career researchers from six African countries with senior collaborators in African and European institutions. Specific Aim 1 is to extend the programme to two further cohorts, with an emphasis on institutions that have limited access to high-performance computing. We will provide access to shared computing resources and training in cluster use, which our first evaluation identified as a binding constraint on sustained research activity.

Specific Aim 2 is to strengthen the mentorship structure. Our previous experience showed that outcomes varied considerably between pairings, and that clear written milestones and shared project plans were associated with better results. In this phase, each mentee will have a written development plan agreed at the start of the programme, and mentors will receive training on supervision in a resource-limited setting. We will track whether these measures reduce the variation in outcomes.

Specific Aim 3 is to evaluate the programme over a longer period. We will follow participants for four years, using the mixed-methods design developed in the first phase, and will add measures of professional networks and of the teaching that participants carry out after the programme. Participants will be involved in designing the evaluation, and the results will be shared with the institutions that host them. Significance: capacity building in this field has often been measured by attendance rather than by outcomes that matter to researchers and their institutions. This proposal would generate evidence on what works over a longer period and would give funders a practical model for investment.

Mentors will be supported through a modest stipend and through access to a shared community of practice, since the time commitment is substantial and often unrecognised by host institutions. We will report mentor workload alongside mentee outcomes in each annual report.

The aim of this project is to develop and validate a framework for evaluating generative models of molecules against project-specific criteria, and to test whether models designed under this framework produce candidates that perform better in prospective testing. Specific Aim 1 is to define a set of evaluation criteria with input from medicinal chemists in partner laboratories, covering validity, diversity, distribution similarity, synthetic accessibility and project constraints such as predicted activity and absence of structural alerts. We will publish the criteria before any model is trained, and we will use them to compare five architectures on a common curated dataset.

Specific Aim 2 is to conduct a controlled prospective comparison. For a bacterial efflux pump target, we will select candidate compounds from generated libraries and from conventional screening collections using identical criteria, purchase them, and test them at several concentrations in a blinded assay. We will prespecify the sample size, which we estimate at 120 compounds per arm, to detect a difference in hit rate of 8 percentage points with reasonable power. This design addresses the main weakness of our pilot study, in which the generated compounds were pre-enriched by the authors' own pipeline.

Specific Aim 3 is to quantify the trade-off between novelty and synthetic accessibility across architectures, and to provide users with tools that show this trade-off explicitly. The output will be a model card for each architecture that reports its performance on all criteria, not only on the aggregate score that is usually reported. Significance: generative models are increasingly used to propose compounds, yet prospective evidence that they outperform conventional methods remains limited. This project would provide that evidence under a transparent protocol, and its outputs would be useful to any group deciding whether to use these tools.
